cesari-12-aggregation-055.front: Receiver swap 3Y + payer swap 7Y com netting. Como naive e Euler alocam a PFE nos anos 1–3?
cesari-12-aggregation-055.back:
- Naive: positiva para os dois (ex.: ano 3: 3Y 2,12; 7Y 7,85).
- Euler: negativa para o 3Y e positiva para o 7Y (ano 3: 3Y −2,82; 7Y 12,79).
O 3Y reduz a exposure do 7Y. Após o ano 3 as duas coincidem.

cesari-12-aggregation-056.front: Como alocar exposure de trades colateralizados de forma numericamente estável?
cesari-12-aggregation-056.back: Tratar o collateral como mais uma perna gera resultados instáveis. Melhor: calcular contribuições **sem** collateral; depois a exposure com collateral. A contribuição do CSA é a diferença entre exposure com e sem collateral.

cesari-13-market-credit-001.front: No framework AMC do livro, sob qual medida as distribuições de valor futuro são simuladas, e quais são as três situações em que se precisa de outra medida?

cesari-13-market-credit-002.front: Por que o livro quer obter a distribuição de valor sob uma nova medida via change of measure, e não por uma nova simulação?
cesari-13-market-credit-002.back: Para reaproveitar as mesmas trajetórias e os mesmos valores AMC já calculados sob $\mathbb{N}$. Basta re-ponderar cada cenário pelo Radon-Nikodym $\zeta^{(i)}$. Não há custo de nova simulação nem de novo pricing.

cesari-13-market-credit-004.front: Como se calcula o CDF do valor $V_t$ sob uma medida $\mathbb{P}$ usando apenas amostras simuladas sob $\mathbb{N}$?
cesari-13-market-credit-004.back:
$$F_t^{\mathbb{P}}(v)=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\mathbb{1}\{V_t\le v\}]=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{N}}[\mathbb{1}\{V_t\le v\}\,\zeta_t],\quad \zeta_t=\left.\tfrac{d\mathbb{P}}{d\mathbb{N}}\right|_{\mathcal{F}_t}$$
Empiricamente: média amostral de $\mathbb{1}\{V_t^{(i)}\le v\}\,\zeta_t^{(i)}$.

cesari-13-market-credit-005.front: Depois de obter $\hat F_t^{\mathbb{P}}$ e $\hat F_t^{\mathbb{N}}$, como o livro gera uma amostra de $V_t$ sob $\mathbb{P}$?
cesari-13-market-credit-005.back:
Por quantile mapping: $\tilde V_t^{(i)}=(\hat F_t^{\mathbb{P}})^{-1}\big(\hat F_t^{\mathbb{N}}(V_t^{(i)})\big)$.
Inverte-se $\hat F_t^{\mathbb{P}}$ por interpolação. Na amostra $\{\tilde V_t^{(i)}\}$ calculam-se quantis (PFE) e médias como na amostra original.

cesari-13-market-credit-006.front: Com fatores de risco $Y=RX$ ($X$ Brownian motion em $\mathbb{R}^d$), que escolha de $\gamma_t$ no Radon-Nikodym leva da medida martingale $\mathbb{N}$ à real-world $\mathbb{P}$?
cesari-13-market-credit-006.back:
$$\gamma_t=(R^{\top}R)^{-1}R^{\top}\delta,\quad \delta\in\mathbb{R}^d \text{ constante}$$
Isso adiciona drift $\delta$ a $Y$. Para ir a $\mathbb{P}$, $\delta_i$ = market price of risk do fator $i$.

cesari-13-market-credit-007.front: Para um fator de risco log-normal, a que corresponde o market price of risk $\delta$ usado na mudança para a medida real-world?
cesari-13-market-credit-007.back:
Ao Sharpe ratio: (retorno esperado $-$ taxa livre de risco) / volatilidade.
Ex.: $\delta=0.3$ com $\sigma=30\%$ dá excesso de retorno de $0.3\times0.3=9\%$ a.a.

cesari-13-market-credit-008.front: Quando é especialmente importante estimar exposure sob a medida real-world em vez da risk-neutral?
cesari-13-market-credit-008.back: Quando o underlying tem drift real acentuado. A PFE risk-neutral só tem o drift da taxa livre de risco. Com um drift real forte, o payoff realizado pode ultrapassar a PFE estimada na originação.

cesari-13-market-credit-009.front: No exemplo do forward de petróleo (jul/2007, 100 barris a USD 72), o que aconteceu com a PFE 97.5% risk-neutral, e que lição isso dá?
cesari-13-market-credit-009.back:
A PFE máxima estimada era ~USD 5000. O petróleo chegou a ~USD 130 em jul/2008. O payoff realizado foi ~USD 6000, acima da PFE.
Lição: analisar na originação a exposure com um drift imposto ao driver (aqui $\delta=0.3$, i.e. 9% de excesso de retorno).

cesari-13-market-credit-010.front: Por que o livro trata o drift real-world $\delta$ como um cenário, e não como um parâmetro estimado?
cesari-13-market-credit-010.back: Estimar drift de séries históricas é muito difícil. Além do ruído estatístico, as séries alternam regimes muito diferentes. Logo, $\delta$ serve para ver como a exposure se comporta num regime escolhido.

cesari-13-market-credit-011.front: Em stress testing via change of measure, como o livro representa um conjunto de cenários de stress?
cesari-13-market-credit-011.back: Como medidas $\mathbb{P}_1,\dots,\mathbb{P}_n$. Em cada uma, o driver de risco de interesse recebe um drift $\delta_i$ diferente (crescimento acelerado ou desacelerado). A distribuição de valor sob cada $\mathbb{P}_i$ sai da mesma simulação por re-ponderação.

cesari-13-market-credit-012.front: Dado um conjunto de medidas de stress $\mathcal{P}=\{\mathbb{P}_i\}$, que medida de risco o livro propõe e que propriedade ela tem?
cesari-13-market-credit-012.back:
$$\rho(V)=\sup_{\mathbb{P}_i\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}_i}[V]$$
É uma medida de risco **coerente** (em particular, subaditiva). Calcula-se a média de $V$ sob cada cenário e toma-se a maior.

cesari-13-market-credit-013.front: No exemplo de um trade com driver ouro e um cenário $\mathbb{P}^*$ de alta extrema do ouro, qual é a medida de risco coerente?
cesari-13-market-credit-013.back: $\rho(V_t)=\max\{\mathbb{E}^*(V_t),\,\mathbb{E}(V_t)\}$: a maior entre a média sob o cenário de stress e a média sob a medida original, a cada data $t$.

cesari-13-market-credit-014.front: Segundo a definição do livro, o credit exposure numa data $t$ é a distribuição de qual quantidade, e quando ela coincide com a price exposure?
cesari-13-market-credit-014.back: É a distribuição do valor do trade **condicional ao default da contraparte em $t$**. Coincide com a distribuição não condicional (price exposure) quando o default não altera (ou altera pouco) a distribuição de valor, i.e. valor e qualidade de crédito são independentes.

cesari-13-market-credit-015.front: O que caracteriza right-way e wrong-way exposure?
cesari-13-market-credit-015.back:
A distribuição de valor futuro do trade **não** é independente da qualidade de crédito da contraparte. Condicionar no default muda a distribuição.
- Wrong-way: o default vem junto com exposure maior.
- Right-way: o default vem junto com exposure menor.
(Atenção: o texto do livro define via sinal da correlação com a "credit quality" de forma que parece invertida; os exemplos seguem a definição acima.)

cesari-13-market-credit-016.front: Se você compra de uma contraparte uma call sobre a ação dessa própria contraparte, qual é a exposure no default? E para uma put?
cesari-13-market-credit-016.back:
Call: ~zero, pois a ação (e a call) vale ~nada no default (right-way extremo).
Put: a exposure no default é igual ao notional da opção (wrong-way extremo).

cesari-13-market-credit-017.front: Num trade de petróleo e gás com uma contraparte do setor de commodities, sob que medida se deve analisar a credit exposure?
cesari-13-market-credit-017.back: Sob uma medida em que petróleo e gás têm um drift fortemente negativo. O default da firma é consistente com preços baixos dessas commodities. Condicionar no default equivale a olhar esse regime.

cesari-13-market-credit-018.front: Quais são as duas abordagens do livro para right-way/wrong-way exposure, e qual é a restrição da segunda?
cesari-13-market-credit-018.back:
1. Change of measure: impor um drift escolhido ao driver de risco ligado ao default.
2. Abordagem Merton: correlacionar um fator de mercado gaussiano com o distance-to-default da contraparte.
A abordagem Merton (com o mapeamento $V\to Z$) só funciona se o payoff for monotônico nos fatores de risco.

cesari-13-market-credit-019.front: Na abordagem Merton para wrong-way risk, como se modela o default da contraparte num horizonte fixo?
cesari-13-market-credit-019.back:
$X=\rho Z+\bar\rho\tilde X$, com $Z,\tilde X\sim N(0,1)$ independentes e $\bar\rho=\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$.
Default $\Leftrightarrow X<C$, com $C=\Phi^{-1}(p)$ e $p$ a probabilidade de default no horizonte.
$Z$ é o fator de mercado que move o valor do trade.

cesari-13-market-credit-020.front: Na abordagem Merton para wrong-way risk, qual é a interpretação econômica da variável latente $X$?
cesari-13-market-credit-020.back: O (log-)retorno do valor dos ativos da contraparte, após transformação/re-escala. Default quando o retorno fica abaixo de um nível $C$: ideia de distance-to-default.

cesari-13-market-credit-021.front: Na abordagem Merton, qual é a densidade de $Z$ condicional ao default $\{X<C\}$?
cesari-13-market-credit-021.back:
$$\tilde\phi(z)=\frac{\Phi\!\left(\frac{C-\rho z}{\bar\rho}\right)}{\Phi(C)}\,\phi(z)$$
Vem de Bayes: $\mathbb{P}[Z=z\mid X<C]=\mathbb{P}[X<C\mid Z=z]\,\phi(z)/\mathbb{P}[X<C]$.

cesari-13-market-credit-022.front: Na densidade condicional $\tilde\phi(z)=\phi(z)\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{C-\rho z}{\bar\rho}\right)/\Phi(C)$, qual é a intuição do fator de re-ponderação?
cesari-13-market-credit-022.back: É o Radon-Nikodym $\zeta(Z)=\mathbb{P}[X<C\mid Z]/\mathbb{P}[X<C]$. Cada cenário $z$ ganha peso proporcional a quão mais (ou menos) provável o default é dado esse $z$, relativo à PD marginal.

cesari-13-market-credit-023.front: Na abordagem Merton, para onde se desloca a massa da distribuição condicional de $Z$ quando $\rho>0$? E quando $\rho<0$?
cesari-13-market-credit-023.back:
$\rho>0$: default associado a $X$ baixo e, logo, $Z$ baixo; massa vai para a esquerda.
$\rho<0$: massa vai para a direita.
$\rho=0$: densidade não condicional $\phi$. Com PD pequena (0.1%) e $|\rho|$ alto o deslocamento é grande.

cesari-13-market-credit-024.front: Na abordagem Merton, como se estima o quantil $q$ da exposure condicional ao default a partir das simulações não condicionais $z^{(i)}$?
cesari-13-market-credit-024.back:
Resolve-se em $x_q^{(\rho)}$:
$$q=\sum_{\{z:\,V\le x_q^{(\rho)}\}}\frac{\Phi(\frac{C-\rho z}{\bar\rho})}{\Phi(C)}\Big/\sum_{\{z\}}\frac{\Phi(\frac{C-\rho z}{\bar\rho})}{\Phi(C)}$$
É um quantil ponderado pelos pesos $\zeta(z^{(i)})$. Não exige simular $V$ sob a medida condicional.

cesari-13-market-credit-025.front: No estimador do quantil condicional da abordagem Merton, por que se mantém o denominador $\sum_i \zeta(z^{(i)})$ se o seu valor exato é 1?
cesari-13-market-credit-025.back: Porque a média amostral dos pesos não é exatamente 1. Normalizar garante que a distribuição condicional empírica tenha massa total correta. (O valor teórico é 1 porque a PD condicional média iguala a PD marginal.)

cesari-13-market-credit-026.front: O que é o "inverse problem" da abordagem Merton para wrong-way risk, e para que serve?
cesari-13-market-credit-026.back:
Achar a probabilidade de default da contraparte **condicional a um nível de exposure** observado $V=v$.
Serve para: (i) ver a PD condicional a um cenário de mercado; (ii) mapear a distribuição de preço (função de vários fatores correlacionados) num único fator normal $Z$.

cesari-13-market-credit-027.front: No inverse problem, como se constrói o fator normal $Z$ a partir da distribuição de valor $V$ de um trade com vários fatores de risco?
cesari-13-market-credit-027.back: $Z=\Phi^{-1}(F(V))$, com $F$ o CDF empírico de $V$. $F(V)$ é uniforme; aplicar $\Phi^{-1}$ dá uma normal padrão. Assim $V=G(Z)$ com $G$ monotônica.

cesari-13-market-credit-028.front: No inverse problem, qual é a PD da contraparte condicional a $V=v$?

cesari-13-market-credit-029.front: Quando falha o mapeamento $Z=\Phi^{-1}(F(V))$ do inverse problem, e por quê?
cesari-13-market-credit-029.back: Quando o payoff não é monotônico nos fatores de risco. Aí um mesmo valor $v$ vem de cenários de mercado distintos (ex.: straddle: alta e baixa forte). Não há um $z$ único por nível de exposure.

cesari-13-market-credit-030.front: Para uma call ATM comprada, o que acontece com a exposure (PFE e EPE) quando o default é associado a um drift positivo extra no underlying?
cesari-13-market-credit-030.back: A exposure aumenta. O drift extra torna mais prováveis os cenários com a call in-the-money. No livro: drifts de $0.05\sigma$, $0.1\sigma$, $0.15\sigma$ acima da taxa livre de risco.

cesari-13-market-credit-031.front: Na abordagem Merton aplicada a uma call comprada sobre uma ação, como a exposure varia com $\rho$ entre a ação e a qualidade de crédito da contraparte?
cesari-13-market-credit-031.back: A exposure cai quando $\rho$ sobe. Com $\rho$ alto, default vem com a ação baixa e a call OTM. No limite (call sobre a ação da própria contraparte) a exposure vai a zero. Com $\rho=0$ volta ao quantil não condicional.

cesari-13-market-credit-032.front: Por que, numa estrutura de opções de petróleo com payoff monotônico crescente (long call 105%, short put 95%, long put 90%), a exposure cresce com o drift extra?
cesari-13-market-credit-032.back: Porque o valor da carteira sobe com o preço do petróleo. Drift extra positivo empurra a distribuição para cenários de valor maior. A monotonicidade também permite usar a abordagem Merton.

cesari-13-market-credit-033.front: Num cross-currency swap recebendo USD e pagando GBP com uma firma americana que tem passivos em GBP, a exposure no default é wrong-way ou right-way?
cesari-13-market-credit-033.back: Right-way. Apreciação da GBP aumenta o risco de default da firma. Ao mesmo tempo, como se recebe USD e se paga GBP, a apreciação da GBP reduz o valor do swap. Default vem com exposure menor.

cesari-13-market-credit-034.front: Qual é a diferença de input entre a abordagem Merton e a abordagem change of measure para wrong-way risk?
cesari-13-market-credit-034.back:
Ambas são casos de change of measure.
- Merton: input é a correlação $\rho$ entre o driver gaussiano do trade e o distance-to-default.
- Change of measure: input é um drift escolhido no driver que se acredita causar ou sofrer com o default.

cesari-13-market-credit-035.front: Como o livro estima na prática a correlação $\rho$ da abordagem Merton, e que cuidado recomenda?
cesari-13-market-credit-035.back: Usa a correlação linear entre os retornos da ação da contraparte e os retornos do driver do trade. Como $\rho$ é difícil de estimar, recomenda calcular a exposure para uma faixa de valores de $\rho$ e ver a sensibilidade.

cesari-13-market-credit-036.front: Qual é a vantagem da abordagem change of measure (drift imposto) sobre a Merton para wrong-way risk?
cesari-13-market-credit-036.back: Controle explícito da evolução do driver de risco escolhido: impõe-se diretamente o cenário (ex.: petróleo caindo). A Merton depende de um $\rho$ difícil de estimar e exige payoff monotônico.

cesari-14-pricing-001.front: Por que hedge de counterparty risk via CDS single-name nem sempre é direto? (4 motivos do livro)
cesari-14-pricing-001.back:
1. CDS da contraparte pode ser ilíquido ou sem a maturidade desejada.
2. Não há forma única de definir os notionals dos CDS.
3. O recovery do bond entregue no CDS pouco tem a ver com o recovery do trade hedgeado.
4. Reajustar o perfil de proteção após o início pode ser caro demais.

cesari-14-pricing-002.front: Quando falta liquidez no CDS da contraparte, que instrumento se usa e qual sua limitação?
cesari-14-pricing-002.back:
Índices de crédito (CDX, iTraxx; ABX, CMBX para ABS).
Vantagem: liquidez e custo menor.
Limitação: são genéricos e não pagam a proteção cheia no default da contraparte. Servem sobretudo para hedgear o risco de spread de mercado.

cesari-14-pricing-003.front: Por que comprar uma quantidade fixa de CDS no início do trade é um hedge fraco de counterparty risk? Qual a analogia do livro?
cesari-14-pricing-003.back:
É como hedgear uma opção com quantidade fixa da ação.
A exposure é estocástica; o hedge deve ser dinâmico, para que o valor do portfólio no default iguale $V_\tau^+$.

cesari-14-pricing-004.front: O que é um contingent credit default swap (C-CDS)?
cesari-14-pricing-004.back:
Um contrato que, no default da contraparte, paga exatamente a exposure positiva $V_\tau^+$ do trade (ou portfólio) protegido.
É um derivativo sobre o processo de valor $V_t$.

cesari-14-pricing-005.front: Qual a relação entre CVA e C-CDS?
cesari-14-pricing-005.back:
O CVA é o valor em $t=0$ do C-CDS.
É o custo de montar o portfólio replicante da credit exposure (também chamado *credit charge*).

cesari-14-pricing-006.front: Além de proteger contra default, por que um banco precisa hedgear o CVA?
cesari-14-pricing-006.back:
O CVA entra no P&L do banco.
Por isso é uma fonte grande de volatilidade de P&L, mesmo sem default.

cesari-14-pricing-007.front: Em que o CVA difere da protection leg de um CDS padrão?
cesari-14-pricing-007.back:
CDS padrão paga um valor fixo ajustado pelo recovery.
No CVA o pagamento no default é o valor estocástico do trade, $V_\tau^+$.

cesari-14-pricing-008.front: O que o valor do CVA diz, e o que não diz, sobre o hedge?
cesari-14-pricing-008.back:
Diz quanto custa montar o portfólio que replica a credit exposure.
Não diz como esse portfólio deve ser estruturado.

cesari-14-pricing-009.front: Escreva o CVA em $t=0$ até o horizonte $T$ (forma com expectativa condicional ao default).
cesari-14-pricing-009.back:
$$\mathrm{CVA}_{0,T}=(1-R_V)\int_0^T \mathbb{E}\big[N_u^{-1}V_u^+\,\big|\,\tau=u\big]\,\mathbb{N}(\tau\in(u,u+du))$$
$R_V$: recovery esperado no portfólio; $N$: numeraire; $\tau$: default da contraparte.

cesari-14-pricing-010.front: Na fórmula do CVA, por que a expectativa de $N_u^{-1}V_u^+$ é condicional a $\tau=u$?
cesari-14-pricing-010.back:
Porque o que importa é a exposure no momento do default.
Se $V$ e $\tau$ forem dependentes (wrong/right-way), a exposure condicional difere da não-condicional.

cesari-14-pricing-011.front: Como o livro escreve o CVA em termos de modified EPE e do preço de CDS?
cesari-14-pricing-011.back:
$$\mathrm{CVA}_{0,T}=\frac{1-R_V}{1-R}\int_0^T \mathrm{EPE}^{mod}_u\,d\mathrm{CDS}_u$$
com $\mathrm{EPE}^{mod}_u:=D_{0,u}^{-1}\mathbb{E}[N_u^{-1}V_u^+\mid\tau=u]$ e $\mathrm{CDS}_t:=(1-R)\int_0^t D_{0,u}\,\mathbb{N}(\tau\in(u,u+du))$ (protection leg com maturidade $t$).

cesari-14-pricing-012.front: Na forma $\mathrm{CVA}=\frac{1-R_V}{1-R}\int \mathrm{EPE}^{mod}_u\,d\mathrm{CDS}_u$, por que aparece a razão $\frac{1-R_V}{1-R}$?
cesari-14-pricing-012.back:
$d\mathrm{CDS}_u$ já embute a LGD $(1-R)$ do CDS de mercado.
A razão troca essa LGD pela do trade, $(1-R_V)$. Os dois recoveries em geral diferem.

cesari-14-pricing-013.back:
$\mathbb{E}[N_u^{-1}V_u^+|\tau=u]$ é valor presente.
$D_{0,u}^{-1}$ o leva a valor forward em $u$, porque $d\mathrm{CDS}_u$ já desconta com $D_{0,u}$. Assim não se desconta duas vezes.

cesari-14-pricing-014.front: A fórmula $\int \mathrm{EPE}^{mod}\,d\mathrm{CDS}$ sugere hedgear com uma escada de CDS de várias maturidades. Por que isso falha?
cesari-14-pricing-014.back:
- A escada protege só a exposure esperada original, não o MtM real no default.
- Quando $V_t$ e o spread se movem, o CVA muda.
- Variações de CVA por fatores de mercado (não-spread) ficam sem hedge e geram volatilidade de P&L.

cesari-14-pricing-015.front: Escreva o preço do C-CDS no tempo $t$.
cesari-14-pricing-015.back:
$$\mathrm{CVA}_{t,T}=(1-R_V)N_t\int_t^T \mathbb{E}\big[N_u^{-1}V_u^+\delta_{\tau-u}\,\big|\,\mathcal{F}_t\big]du$$
A expectativa é na lei conjunta de $\tau$ e $V$, pois podem ser dependentes.

cesari-14-pricing-016.front: Qual a ideia central do livro para hedgear counterparty risk dinamicamente?
cesari-14-pricing-016.back:
Tratar o C-CDS como um derivativo sobre $V_t$.
Aplica-se a ele as estratégias usuais de hedge de derivativos (delta, gamma, portfólio self-financing).

cesari-14-pricing-017.front: Para avaliar o C-CDS como super-product, que três distribuições é preciso simular?
cesari-14-pricing-017.back:
1. Distribuição de preço do portfólio subjacente $V_t$.
2. Distribuição do numeraire $N_t$.
3. Tempos de default $\tau$ da contraparte.

cesari-14-pricing-018.front: No AMC do C-CDS, qual o payoff na data discretizada $T_i$?
cesari-14-pricing-018.back:
$$\Pi_{CCDS}(T_i)=V_{T_i}^+\,\mathbb{1}_{\tau\in\,]T_{i-1},T_i]}$$
Paga a exposure positiva se o default cai no intervalo.

cesari-14-pricing-019.front: Na regressão AMC do C-CDS, quais observables devem entrar no mínimo?
cesari-14-pricing-019.back:
1. Spreads de CDS simulados da contraparte.
2. A distribuição de preço $V$ do portfólio.

cesari-14-pricing-020.front: Que vantagem o livro destaca em avaliar o C-CDS por Monte Carlo?
cesari-14-pricing-020.back:
A correlação entre $V$ e $\tau$ entra automaticamente.
A distribuição de preços já é computada condicional ao default da contraparte.

cesari-14-pricing-021.front: Qual o payoff do C-CDS numa swap payer (paga fixo $K$, recebe float) com maturidade $T$?
cesari-14-pricing-021.back:
$$\Pi_{CCDS}(T_i)=A_{T_i,T}\,(s_{T_i,T}-K)^+\,\mathbb{1}_{\tau\in\,]T_{i-1},T_i]}$$
$A$: annuity; $s$: par rate. A exposure é um payoff de swaption.

cesari-14-pricing-022.front: No exemplo do livro (swap USD 10 anos, notional 1 bi, CDS flat 130 bp), qual a lição de comparar CVA inicial com o PFE 97.5% do C-CDS?
cesari-14-pricing-022.back:
CVA inicial ≈ 8.4 mi USD, mas pode chegar a ≈ 22 mi USD a 97.5%.
O próprio CVA tem risco de juros e de spread relevante; precisa ser hedgeado.

cesari-14-pricing-023.front: Qual a aproximação rápida de CVA para uma swap at-the-money?
cesari-14-pricing-023.back:
$$\mathrm{CVA}_T\simeq\frac{2T}{3}\,\mathrm{EPE}_{max}\,s_T$$
$s_T$: spread de CDS da contraparte. Exemplo: $100\times\frac{2}{3}\times0.013\times10\approx 8.6$ mi USD, próximo do 8.4 do MC.

cesari-14-pricing-024.front: Ao aplicar o hedge delta-gamma a um C-CDS, que três tipos de instrumento ou risco aparecem?
cesari-14-pricing-024.back:
1. CDS na contraparte (risco de crédito).
2. Instrumentos nos fatores de mercado que movem a exposure.
3. Risco de correlação entre drivers (cross-gammas).

cesari-14-pricing-025.front: Por que o risco de correlação entre drivers de um C-CDS é difícil de hedgear?
cesari-14-pricing-025.back: Faltam instrumentos que cubram as derivadas segundas cruzadas (cross-gammas).

cesari-14-pricing-026.front: No optimal static hedge, que objetivo o livro propõe como exemplo para escolher os pesos $\alpha$?
cesari-14-pricing-026.back:
Maximizar o Sharpe ratio do P&L do hedge, usando a gain process $G_\alpha(t)$ escalada pelo numeraire:
$$\max_\alpha \frac{M(t,1)}{\sqrt{M(t,2)-M(t,1)^2}}$$
$M(t,k)$: k-ésimo momento de $G_\alpha(t)$.

cesari-14-pricing-027.front: Quais as três vantagens do optimal static hedge apontadas pelo livro? E o custo?
cesari-14-pricing-027.back:
Vantagens: (i) aceita várias funções objetivo, não só delta-flat; (ii) minimiza rebalanceamento; (iii) combina com hedge dinâmico.
Custo: exige distribuições de preço do portfólio inteiro no tempo; é computacionalmente pesado.

cesari-14-pricing-028.front: Com AMC, como se obtêm sensitivities do CVA sem bump-and-reprice?
cesari-14-pricing-028.back:
O AMC estima a distribuição de preço como função de variáveis estocásticas escolhidas.
Deriva-se essa função regredida em relação às variáveis. Custo: um passo extra de regressão.

cesari-14-pricing-029.front: Qual a limitação e qual o cuidado das sensitivities de CVA obtidas por regressão AMC?
cesari-14-pricing-029.back:
Limitação: não dá sensitivity a quantidades não-estocásticas.
Cuidado: dá a sensitivity ao observable escolhido, não a um fator isolado. Para manter os outros fatores fixos, é preciso de-correlacionar (Sect. 4.5.3).

cesari-14-pricing-030.front: Qual em geral a principal fonte de variação do CVA, e como se hedgeia?
cesari-14-pricing-030.back:
O credit spread da contraparte.
Hedge com CDS da contraparte, decomposto em time buckets que casam com as maturidades de CDS disponíveis. Sensitivity: finite difference na eq. (14.2).

cesari-14-pricing-031.front: Se a contraparte não tem CDS líquido e se hedgeia com índices, que risco fica aberto?
cesari-14-pricing-031.back:
O risco idiossincrático da contraparte.
O índice cobre só risco genérico ou setorial.

cesari-14-pricing-032.front: Por que o livro prefere hedgear o market risk do CVA com futuros e opções listados?
cesari-14-pricing-032.back: Para não adicionar counterparty risk com outra contraparte.

cesari-14-pricing-033.front: Por que o risco de correlação market/credit do CVA é difícil de hedgear, e como se lida com ele na prática?
cesari-14-pricing-033.back:
Há várias formas realistas de modelar a dependência, e cada uma dá um preço de C-CDS diferente.
Na prática se estuda um range de cenários de dependência em vez de fixar um valor.

cesari-14-pricing-034.front: Para um portfólio de juros ou FX, quando a correlação market/credit não pode ser ignorada?
cesari-14-pricing-034.back:
Quando a contraparte é soberana.
Fora disso, o livro diz que pode ser ignorada com segurança.

cesari-14-pricing-035.front: Qual o efeito de break clauses no CVA, e qual o risco prático?
cesari-14-pricing-035.back:
Reduzem o C-CDS: não há fluxo a proteger após a break date. No portfólio, agem como amortização do notional.
Risco: o banco pode não exercer o break (relação com o cliente). Aí precisa comprar mais proteção e recalcular o CVA.

cesari-14-pricing-036.front: Com colateral, margin call diária e threshold zero, por que o CVA não vai a zero?
cesari-14-pricing-036.back:
No default, o detentor precisa liquidar o colateral, o que leva tempo.
Nesse período o valor do trade muda: close-out risk. Com colateral ilíquido, o período é maior e o risco também.

cesari-14-pricing-037.front: Quando o efeito de wrong-way risk no C-CDS é mais forte?
cesari-14-pricing-037.back:
Quando o portfólio subjacente contém instrumentos de crédito.
No default da contraparte, spreads de nomes correlacionados saltam e mudam $V$ de imediato.

cesari-14-pricing-038.front: Que instrumentos seriam necessários, em princípio, para hedgear um C-CDS sobre portfólio de crédito correlacionado com a contraparte?
cesari-14-pricing-038.back: Instrumentos sensíveis a correlação, como tranches de CDO que envolvam a contraparte e os nomes subjacentes.

cesari-14-pricing-039.front: Como reconciliar a distribuição condicional ao default (cap. 13) com o C-CDS, e qual o custo?
cesari-14-pricing-039.back:
Extraindo, na simulação, os paths em que a contraparte defaulta.
Como default é raro, isso exige muito mais simulações.

cesari-14-pricing-040.front: Com $V$ independente de $\tau$, como replicar o C-CDS de uma swap vanilla com swaptions e CDS?
cesari-14-pricing-040.back:
$$\mathrm{CCDS}_t\simeq\sum_{t_i>t}\mathrm{Swaption}(t,t_i,T)\,P(t,t_{i-1},t_i)$$
Swaptions com expiry $t_i$, strike = taxa fixa da swap, pesadas pela probabilidade incremental de default.

cesari-14-pricing-041.front: Quais as duas leituras equivalentes do C-CDS de uma swap vanilla (sem correlação)?
cesari-14-pricing-041.back:
1. Um CDS amortizante até $T$ com notional igual ao perfil de modified EPE.
2. Uma strip de swaptions com notionals iguais às probabilidades incrementais de default.
Logo, o hedge dinâmico usa swaptions e CDS.

cesari-14-pricing-042.front: Por que a discretization schedule pode distorcer o CVA de uma swap com cupons?
cesari-14-pricing-042.back:
A exposure cai no pagamento do cupom.
- Datas logo antes do pagamento: superestima o CVA.
- Datas logo depois: subestima.

cesari-14-pricing-043.front: Como o livro corrige o efeito dos cupons no C-CDS de uma swap?
cesari-14-pricing-043.back:
Soma uma strip de caplets nas datas de cupom $T_i$, pesados pela probabilidade de default no intervalo:
$$+\sum_{T_i>t}\mathrm{Caplet}(t,T_i)\,P(t,T_{i-1},T_i)$$

cesari-14-pricing-044.front: Num forward (equity swap) colateralizado diariamente, threshold zero, sobre ação ilíquida, qual o valor em $t=0$ do close-out risk por ação?
cesari-14-pricing-044.back:
$$\mathbb{E}\big[N_t^{-1}(S_t-S_{t-\delta})^+\big]$$
$\delta$: duração do close-out. Hedgear isso é hedgear um payoff tipo cliquet.

cesari-14-pricing-045.front: No case study (forward EUR/USD 20 anos, CDS 300 bp), quanto se perderia hedgeando só o spread, e por quê?
cesari-14-pricing-045.back:
CVA foi de ≈ 10 para ≈ 24 mi USD em um ano, com o spread parado. Perda ≈ 14 mi USD.
Causa: a queda do EUR/USD aumentou a exposure; o hedge de CDS não cobre isso.

cesari-14-pricing-046.front: No case study, o valor do trade em 2009 estava fora do PFE calculado em 2008?
cesari-14-pricing-046.back:
Não. Estava dentro do PFE de 2008.
Mas os novos perfis de EPE/PFE de 2009 saíram dos limites de 2008. O CVA mudou muito sem nenhum evento extremo.

cesari-14-pricing-047.front: No case study, como o livro hedgeou o FX risk do CVA, e com que resultado?
cesari-14-pricing-047.back:
Futuros de EUR/USD de um ano (líquidos, sem novo counterparty risk): long ≈ 37 mi EUR, pelo delta do CVA de ≈ −37 mi USD.
Resultado: lucro ≈ 1 mi USD contra perda de 14 mi USD sem hedge.

cesari-14-pricing-048.front: No case study com spread subindo de 300 para 400 bp, compare os resultados: sem hedge, só CDS, hedge completo.
cesari-14-pricing-048.back:
- Sem hedge: perda ≈ 18 mi USD.
- Só CDS (estático): perda ≈ 16 mi USD.
- FX + CDS: perda ≈ 1 mi USD.

cesari-14-pricing-049.front: No case study, o portfólio tem 20 anos mas só o CDS de 5 anos é líquido. Como se dimensiona o hedge de spread?
cesari-14-pricing-049.back:
Iguala-se o credit delta do CVA (≈ 20 kUSD/bp) ao delta do CDS 5Y (≈ 400 USD/bp por 1 mi USD).
Notional ≈ 50 mi USD.

cesari-14-pricing-050.front: Num cálculo clássico de CVA (EPE estático × spread), qual componente do hedge é difícil de computar e qual é difícil de executar?
cesari-14-pricing-050.back:
Componente de mercado: difícil de computar (exige sensitivities do EPE aos fatores), mas usa instrumentos listados.
Componente de crédito: fácil de computar, mas usa CDS OTC, nem sempre disponível em todos os nomes e maturidades.

cesari-14-pricing-051.front: Que risco adicional do CVA o livro destaca para portfólios dominados por FX, e como modelá-lo?
cesari-14-pricing-051.back:
Vega risk (movimentos da vol implícita).
Para hedgear, inclui-se a volatilidade como driver estocástico no C-CDS (modelo de stochastic vol).

cesari-14-pricing-052.front: No cap. 14, o CVA considera o default de quem? Que ajustes ficam de fora?
cesari-14-pricing-052.back:
Só da contraparte (CVA unilateral). O capítulo não trata o próprio default do banco.
(Prática de 2009. Hoje a contabilidade (IFRS 13) também reconhece o risco de crédito próprio (DVA), e os bancos gerenciam outros XVAs, como FVA.)

d1-01-physical-001.front: Client is long a TRS paying SOFR + spread; desk funds the hedge at SOFR + x. Why can you ignore SOFR when pricing?
d1-01-physical-001.back:
Client pays SOFR and the desk pays SOFR to fund. SOFR cancels.
Only spreads over SOFR matter, in bp per year on notional.

d1-01-physical-002.front: Name the five cost lines of holding a physical hedge for a client long TRS.
d1-01-physical-002.back:
1. Secured funding (repo).
2. Unsecured funding of the haircut.
3. Leverage (SLR) charge.
4. Counterparty capital on the client swap.
5. Sec lending income (negative cost).

d1-01-physical-003.front: Who funds the desk's inventory, and how is the desk charged?
d1-01-physical-003.back:
Treasury / ALM funds it and charges an internal funds transfer price (FTP).
The FTP covers debt cost plus a charge for scarce balance sheet.

d1-01-physical-004.front: Shares worth 10m, repo haircut 15%. How is the position funded?
d1-01-physical-004.back:
8.5m secured at the repo rate.
1.5m (the haircut) unsecured at the firm's higher unsecured rate.
The haircut sets the weights of the blend.

d1-01-physical-005.front: Repo at SOFR + 30 bp, unsecured at SOFR + 100 bp, haircut 15%. Funding cost in bp?

d1-01-physical-006.front: Formula for the leverage (SLR) charge on a position, and the intuition.
d1-01-physical-006.back:
$\text{charge} = \text{exposure ratio} \times \text{leverage \%} \times (K_e - \text{debt cost})$.
Equity replaces debt in funding the asset. Debt cost is already in the funding lines, so charge only the excess return equity demands.

d1-01-physical-007.front: Physical stock, leverage requirement 4.5%, $K_e$ 12%, debt cost 5%. Leverage charge?
d1-01-physical-007.back:
$100\% \times 4.5\% \times 7\% = 31.5$ bp.
Usually the largest line of the physical hedge.

d1-01-physical-008.front: Why does a safe, liquid stock still cost a lot of balance sheet at a G-SIB?
d1-01-physical-008.back:
The SLR counts every asset at full size, with no risk weighting.
So 10m of a GC name uses the same leverage exposure as 10m of a risky one.

d1-01-physical-009.front: What did the US eSLR rule effective 1 Apr 2026 change for G-SIB holding companies?
d1-01-physical-009.back:
Before: 3% + fixed 2% buffer = 5%.
After: 3% + half the Method 1 GSIB surcharge (usually below 5%).
It **lowered** the leverage charge on balance-sheet-heavy trades.

d1-01-physical-010.front: Leverage requirement drops from 5% to 4.5% ($K_e$ − debt = 7%). Change in the leverage line?
d1-01-physical-010.back:
$5\% \times 7\% = 35$ bp → $4.5\% \times 7\% = 31.5$ bp.
−3.5 bp per year on notional.

d1-01-physical-011.front: Leverage charge vs counterparty capital charge: what drives each?
d1-01-physical-011.back:
Leverage: total assets (SLR), no risk weighting.
Counterparty capital: risk-weighted exposure to the client defaulting on the swap.
Two different constraints, often charged separately.

d1-01-physical-012.front: Who lends the desk's long inventory to shorts, and what does the desk get?
d1-01-physical-012.back:
Prime Brokerage / Sec Lending lends it and earns the borrow fee.
The desk receives a share of that fee as income.

d1-01-physical-013.front: Illustrative stack: repo 25.5, haircut 15, leverage 31.5, capital 10, lending −10. Client pays SOFR + 50. Desk P&L?
d1-01-physical-013.back:
Cost $= 72$ bp. P&L $= 50 - 72 = -22$ bp ≈ −22k USD/yr on 10m.
50 bp does not cover a standalone physical hedge.

d1-01-physical-014.front: Same stack, but the name goes special: fee 300 bp, desk keeps half. Desk P&L?
d1-01-physical-014.back:
Lending income $= -150$ bp. Cost $= 82 - 150 = -68$ bp (net income).
P&L $= 50 + 68 = +118$ bp ≈ +118k USD/yr.
On a special, the long hedge pays for itself.

d1-01-physical-015.front: Decision rule: when does a physical hedge make money?
d1-01-physical-015.back:
client spread ≥ funding spread + leverage charge + counterparty capital − lending income.
If not: internalize, or hedge synthetically.

d1-01-physical-016.front: Pitfall: why not charge full $K_e$ on the capital slice?
d1-01-physical-016.back:
Capital also replaces debt that the funding lines already charged.
Full $K_e$ double-counts the debt cost. Use $K_e$ − debt cost.

d1-02-synthetic-001.front: Name the hedge routes for a client long single-stock TRS.
d1-02-synthetic-001.back:
1. Internalize against a client short.
2. Buy the stock (physical).
3. Swap facility with a street dealer.
4. Listed options: long call + short put.
(Index: futures.)

d1-02-synthetic-002.front: Why is internalization the first route to check?
d1-02-synthetic-002.back:
Netting a client long against a client short needs no hedge, no shares, no balance sheet.
Cost is near zero; the desk earns the spread on both sides.

d1-02-synthetic-003.front: Why does a synthetic hedge use less balance sheet than physical?
d1-02-synthetic-003.back:
Physical stock counts 100% of notional in the SLR denominator.
A derivative counts replacement cost + PFE add-on (SA-CCR), e.g. ~15% for a margined 1y swap.

d1-02-synthetic-004.front: Leverage charge on a margined swap: exposure 15%, leverage 4.5%, $K_e$ − debt 7%?

d1-02-synthetic-005.front: Why can a dealer quote a swap facility below your physical hedge cost?
d1-02-synthetic-005.back:
1. Cheaper funding or balance sheet than yours.
2. It nets your trade against its own client flow.
Its spread is your cost; add your own leverage and capital lines.

d1-02-synthetic-006.front: To hedge a client long, which options combo does the desk buy?
d1-02-synthetic-006.back:
Long call + short put, same strike and expiry = synthetic long forward.
Long put + short call is synthetic **short**.

d1-02-synthetic-007.front: What is the real cost of a synthetic forward from listed options? Why not the premium?
d1-02-synthetic-007.back:
The premium buys an asset worth it, so it is not a cost.
The cost is the **implied financing rate** inside the option prices, versus your own funding.

d1-02-synthetic-008.front: Write put-call parity with dividends and say what you solve for.
d1-02-synthetic-008.back:
$C - P = S - PV(\text{div}) - K \cdot DF(T)$.
Solve for $DF(T)$ → implied financing rate. Intuition: the combo is the stock with deferred payment.

d1-02-synthetic-009.front: How does the options market reveal borrow cost on a hard-to-borrow name?
d1-02-synthetic-009.back:
Shorts can't borrow the stock, so they sell synthetic forwards instead.
The implied forward drops below theoretical; the gap prices the borrow fee.

d1-02-synthetic-010.front: Reversal vs conversion: what is each?
d1-02-synthetic-010.back:
Conversion: long stock + long put + short call (synthetic short on top of stock).
Reversal: short stock + long call + short put.
Switching a physical long to synthetic = sell stock, buy call, sell put.

d1-02-synthetic-011.front: What is a switch, and three reasons to do one?
d1-02-synthetic-011.back:
Move a hedge between physical and synthetic with no delta change.
1. Name goes special → go physical, earn lending income.
2. Balance-sheet pressure (reporting dates) → go synthetic.
3. Relative cost moves.

d1-02-synthetic-012.front: How is a switch executed without market risk?
d1-02-synthetic-012.back:
Trade both legs as one package at one price.
Dealer: sell shares and enter the swap at the same price. Options: reversal. Index: EFP (exchange for physical).

d1-02-synthetic-013.front: When is a switch worth doing?
d1-02-synthetic-013.back: When the saving over the remaining tenor exceeds the bid-ask paid on both legs.

d1-02-synthetic-014.front: Client short TRS, desk short the stock. Why is borrow a term-mismatch risk?
d1-02-synthetic-014.back:
Client spread is fixed for the swap's term.
The borrow fee floats daily and the lender can recall the shares.
Term liability, overnight funding.

d1-02-synthetic-015.front: Four ways a desk manages borrow risk on short swaps.
d1-02-synthetic-015.back:
1. Term borrow (lock the fee, pay a premium).
2. Repricing rights in the confirm.
3. ISDA disruption events: increased cost / loss of stock borrow.
4. Pricing buffer on high-utilization names.

d1-02-synthetic-016.front: Decision rule: how to choose the hedge route?
d1-02-synthetic-016.back:
All-in cost = spread + exposure ratio × leverage % × ($K_e$ − debt) + capital − lending income + roll/execution.
Pick the lowest. Recompute when an input moves.

d1-03-divs-index-001.front: What is the DPR on a single-stock TRS, and where does the desk's dividend risk come from?
d1-03-divs-index-001.back:
Dividend pass-through ratio: the share of the dividend paid to the client (e.g. 100% gross, 70%).
Desk P&L = dividend received net of tax − dividend paid under the DPR.

d1-03-divs-index-002.front: GTR vs NTR index: how are dividends treated?
d1-03-divs-index-002.back:
Both reinvest dividends in the index level.
GTR: gross. NTR: net of the provider's standard withholding rate.

d1-03-divs-index-003.front: Why can an NTR index swap generate a dividend edge for the desk?
d1-03-divs-index-003.back:
If the firm's real withholding is lower than the index provider's rate (treaty, structure), the difference is profit.
Part is passed to clients through a tighter spread. It is a tax-yield enhancement, not a funding benefit.

d1-03-divs-index-004.front: Why must index rebalance trades be executed at the close?
d1-03-divs-index-004.back:
Client swaps and the index use the official closing price.
Cap weights depend on spot, so the desk executes the pro-forma basket at the close, usually via the closing auction.

d1-03-divs-index-005.front: What is restrike risk on an index rebalance?
d1-03-divs-index-005.back:
Slippage between the desk's execution prices and the official close.
Trading early reduces market impact but adds this slippage: a trade-off.

d1-01-physical-017.back:
**GC** (general collateral): easy to borrow, fee of a few bp to ~30 bp per year.
**Special**: scarce supply or heavy short demand, fee can reach hundreds or thousands of bp.

d1-01-physical-018.front: What is utilization in sec lending, and why do traders watch it?
d1-01-physical-018.back:
Utilization = shares on loan / lendable supply.
High utilization means little spare supply: fees can jump and recalls hurt more. It leads fee moves.

d1-01-physical-019.front: Cash collateral of 4.30%, borrow fee 25 bp. What rebate does the borrower receive? And with a fee of 6%?
d1-01-physical-019.back:
Rebate = cash reinvestment rate − fee.
GC: $4.30\% - 0.25\% = 4.05\%$.
Special: $4.30\% - 6\% = -1.70\%$. A negative rebate: the borrower pays on top of giving up interest.

d1-01-physical-020.front: What is a recall, and what happens if the borrower cannot return the shares?
d1-01-physical-020.back:
The lender asks for its shares back (e.g. to sell or to vote).
The borrower must return them, borrow elsewhere, or face a **buy-in**: shares bought in the market at the borrower's cost.

d1-01-physical-021.front: What is days to cover, and what does a high value signal?
d1-01-physical-021.back:
Short interest / average daily volume.
High days to cover: shorts need many days to exit. Squeeze risk, and a candidate for going special.

d1-01-physical-022.front: Why does Treasury charge more for term funding than for overnight funding?
d1-01-physical-022.back:
Locking cash for longer has a liquidity premium and the bank's credit spread grows with tenor.
A desk that funds a 1y swap overnight carries rollover risk. Term funding removes it at a cost.

d1-01-physical-023.front: Funding consumer vs funding provider: which desks are which?
d1-01-physical-023.back:
**Consumers** need cash: long inventory (Delta One hedges, PB margin loans).
**Providers** bring cash in: structured note issuance, client short proceeds, deposits.
Treasury nets them and charges or credits each desk through FTP.

d1-01-physical-024.front: What drives the bank's unsecured funding spread, and where does it show up in pricing?
d1-01-physical-024.back:
The bank's own credit spread (default risk plus liquidity premium).
It prices the unsecured part of every funded position (e.g. the repo haircut) and drives FVA on uncollateralized derivatives.

d1-01-physical-025.front: How does the SLR define the leverage ratio?
d1-01-physical-025.back:
$\text{SLR} = \dfrac{\text{Tier 1 capital}}{\text{total leverage exposure}}$.
Exposure = on-balance-sheet assets + derivative exposure (SA-CCR) + off-balance-sheet items. No risk weights.

d1-02-synthetic-017.front: Which signals would warn you that a name may go special?
d1-02-synthetic-017.back:
1. Rising utilization.
2. Rising fee or falling rebate.
3. Recalls.
4. Event catalysts: M&A, convertible issuance, index deletion, short-seller reports.
5. Options-implied forward trading below theoretical.

d1-02-synthetic-018.front: Client long swap on a name that goes special. Who benefits and why?
d1-02-synthetic-018.back:
The desk, if hedged physically: it can lend the shares at a high fee.
The client spread is fixed, so the desk keeps the extra lending income.

d1-02-synthetic-019.front: Client short swap: what does the client receive on the financing leg?
d1-02-synthetic-019.back:
SOFR − spread (a short rebate).
The spread covers the desk's borrow fee. On a special name the spread can exceed SOFR, so the client pays.

d1-03-divs-index-006.front: Ex-date, record date, pay date: which one decides who gets the dividend, and what happens to the price?
d1-03-divs-index-006.back:
The **ex-date**: whoever holds the stock before it gets the dividend.
On the ex-date the price drops by about the dividend.
Swap confirms usually fix the dividend amount on the ex-date and pay it on the pay date (check the confirm).

d1-03-divs-index-007.front: Foreign stock, treaty withholding 15%. Client TRS with DPR 100% gross, desk hedged physically. Dividend 2.00. Desk P&L on the dividend?
d1-03-divs-index-007.back:
Desk receives $2.00 \times 85\% = 1.70$ and pays $2.00$.
Loss of 0.30 per share. Fix: set DPR at the net rate (85%) or price the gap into the spread.

d1-03-divs-index-008.back:
A US tax rule: a **dividend equivalent** paid to a non-US person on a derivative referencing US stocks is a US-source dividend.
Withholding: 30%, unless a treaty reduces it.

d1-03-divs-index-009.back:
Specified equity-linked instruments with delta ≥ 0.8 at issuance (delta-one), e.g. TRS on US stocks.
Exceptions exist (e.g. qualified indices). The phase-in for lower-delta instruments has been deferred several times.

d1-03-divs-index-010.front: Does a price-return swap on a US stock escape §871(m)?
d1-03-divs-index-010.back:
No, if its pricing reflects expected dividends.
That implicit dividend counts as a dividend equivalent.

d1-03-divs-index-011.front: Why did §871(m) change swap demand from non-US clients?
d1-03-divs-index-011.back:
Before it, swaps let non-US investors receive US dividend economics with no withholding.
After it, a delta-one swap on US stocks withholds like the physical stock. The tax edge disappeared.

d1-03-divs-index-012.front: What is a QDD (qualified derivatives dealer)?
d1-03-divs-index-012.back:
A dealer that takes primary withholding responsibility on the dividend equivalents it pays.
In exchange it is not withheld on dividends it receives as a hedger. This avoids cascading withholding.

d1-03-divs-index-013.front: How are special (extraordinary) dividends usually treated in swaps and indices?
d1-03-divs-index-013.back:
Often as an adjustment event (to notional, strike or index divisor), not as an ordinary dividend flow.
The confirm or index rules define "extraordinary". Read them: this is a common source of breaks.

d1-03-divs-index-014.front: Why do structured product desks end up long dividends, and how do they hedge?
d1-03-divs-index-014.back:
Their delta hedges on price-return-linked notes (e.g. autocallables) gain when realized dividends exceed what was priced, and lose when dividends fall.
They hedge by selling dividend futures or dividend swaps. Delta One / dividend trading is a natural counterparty.

d1-03-divs-index-015.front: What does an index dividend future pay?
d1-03-divs-index-015.back:
The sum of ordinary gross dividends, in index points, with ex-dates inside the contract year (e.g. Euro Stoxx 50 dividend futures).
It isolates dividend risk from price risk.

d1-03-divs-index-016.front: Index 5000, financing 5%, 3-month future at 5040 (simple interest). Implied dividends?
d1-03-divs-index-016.back:
$F = S(1+rT) - D \Rightarrow D = S(1+rT) - F$.
$D = 5000 \times 1.0125 - 5040 = 22.5$ index points (future value).
With known financing, futures reveal dividends; with known dividends, they reveal financing.

d1-04-index-events-001.front: Name the three key dates of an index change.
d1-04-index-events-001.back:
1. **Announcement**: the provider publishes the change.
2. **Effective date**: the change takes effect after the close of the prior trading day.
3. Between them, the **pro-forma** composition is known and trackers plan their trades.

d1-04-index-events-002.front: When do S&P 500 and MSCI quarterly rebalances take effect?
d1-04-index-events-002.back:
S&P: after the close on the third Friday of March, June, September and December.
MSCI: as of the close of the last business day of February, May, August and November.

d1-04-index-events-003.front: Besides scheduled reviews, which events change an index?
d1-04-index-events-003.back:
M&A (deletion at deal close), spin-offs, IPO fast entries, share count changes (buybacks, issuance) and free-float changes.
These are ad hoc and can be announced with little notice.

d1-04-index-events-004.front: You hold a cap-weighted index in index share proportions. The prices move. Do you need to trade?
d1-04-index-events-004.back:
No. Cap weights move with prices, and so do your holdings. A cap-weighted index is self-rebalancing.
You trade only for composition, share-count or float changes.

d1-04-index-events-005.front: Equal-weight index: what must happen at each rebalance?
d1-04-index-events-005.back:
Weights drift with prices, so the tracker sells recent winners and buys recent losers to restore equal weights.
More turnover than cap-weighted, and predictable flow.

d1-04-index-events-006.front: Who trades an index event at the close?
d1-04-index-events-006.back:
1. Passive funds and ETFs (tracking error vs the close).
2. Desks hedging index swaps and futures.
3. Active managers and arbitrageurs who pre-position.
4. Liquidity providers who offset auction imbalances.

d1-04-index-events-007.front: How does a closing auction work?
d1-04-index-events-007.back:
Orders accumulate before the close. The exchange computes one price that maximizes matched volume.
All matched orders trade at that price, which becomes the official close.

d1-04-index-events-008.back:
**MOC** (market-on-close): executes at the closing price, whatever it is.
**LOC** (limit-on-close): executes at the close only if the price is within the limit.

d1-04-index-events-009.front: What is imbalance information in the US closing auction, and when does order entry stop?
d1-04-index-events-009.back:
The exchange publishes the paired volume and the net buy or sell imbalance in the final minutes.
MOC/LOC entry closes about 3:50 pm ET on NYSE and Nasdaq. After that, mostly orders that offset the imbalance are accepted.

d1-04-index-events-010.front: What is the "index effect" around additions?
d1-04-index-events-010.back:
Added stocks tend to rise between announcement and effective date as pre-positioners buy, and often give back part of it afterwards.
Deletions show the mirror pattern. It is a cost for trackers and a risk for pre-positioners.

d1-04-index-events-011.back:
The desk guarantees the client the official closing price on a basket.
The client gets zero tracking error. The desk takes the execution risk and charges for it.

d1-04-index-events-012.front: Index add: desk must buy 1,000,000 shares at the close. It buys 300,000 early at an average of 50.40. Close is 50.00. Restrike P&L?
d1-04-index-events-012.back:
Remaining 700,000 trade in the auction at the close: no slippage.
Early fills: $300{,}000 \times (50.00 - 50.40) = -120{,}000$ USD.

d1-04-index-events-013.front: How does a desk decide how much to trade before the close vs in the auction?
d1-04-index-events-013.back:
Trade-off: more in the auction means more price impact on the close; more early means more restrike slippage.
Size the early share against expected auction depth and the stock's volatility to the close.

d1-04-index-events-014.back:
Trading the futures against the underlying basket when the future deviates from fair value.
Rich future: buy basket, sell future (cash-and-carry). Cheap future: the reverse.

d1-04-index-events-015.front: How do ETF creation and redemption keep the price near NAV?
d1-04-index-events-015.back:
Authorized participants deliver the basket to the ETF and receive new shares (creation), or the reverse (redemption).
If the ETF trades above NAV they create and sell; below NAV they buy and redeem.

d1-04-index-events-016.front: Free-float factor: what is it and why does it matter for rebalances?
d1-04-index-events-016.back:
The fraction of shares available to public investors (excludes strategic holders).
Index weights use float-adjusted shares. A float change moves the weight with no add or delete.

d1-05-products-001.back:
The payoff is linear in the underlying: delta ≈ 1, no optionality.
Examples: TRS, forwards, futures, ETFs, cash equities.

d1-05-products-002.front: Describe the two legs of an equity TRS.
d1-05-products-002.back:
**Equity leg**: price return of the underlying + dividends × DPR.
**Financing leg**: notional × (benchmark + spread) × day count.
The client long receives the equity leg and pays the financing leg.

d1-05-products-003.front: Notional 10m, SOFR 4.30%, spread 50 bp, period 91 days, Act/360. Financing leg payment?

d1-05-products-004.front: What is a reset on a TRS, and why do desks use them?
d1-05-products-004.back:
At each reset the swap settles its MTM and the notional resets to the current value.
It cuts counterparty exposure and keeps the financing on the current notional.

d1-05-products-005.front: Fixed-quantity vs fixed-notional swap: what changes at a reset?
d1-05-products-005.back:
Fixed quantity: the share count stays; notional moves with price.
Fixed notional: the share count changes to keep notional constant, so the hedge must trade at each reset.

d1-05-products-006.front: What is the independent amount (initial margin) on a client TRS?
d1-05-products-006.back:
Collateral the client posts upfront, e.g. 10–20% of notional.
It covers price moves before the desk can close out, and sets the client's leverage.

d1-05-products-007.back:
Price return pays only price moves; the client gives up dividends, so pricing usually includes them (lower financing or a forward-like level).
Total return passes dividends through the DPR.

d1-05-products-008.front: Why do clients use swaps instead of buying the stock?
d1-05-products-008.back:
1. Leverage without a margin loan.
2. Access to markets without local custody or settlement.
3. Easy shorts.
4. One master agreement for many lines.
Trade-offs: no voting rights, counterparty risk, and tax rules such as §871(m).

d1-05-products-009.front: Cash prime brokerage vs synthetic prime.
d1-05-products-009.back:
Cash PB: the client owns the shares, financed by a margin loan; shorts via stock borrow.
Synthetic prime: the client holds portfolio swaps; the bank owns the hedges. Same economics, different balance sheet, legal and tax treatment.

d1-05-products-010.front: Equity forward price with a discrete dividend (simple interest). Stock 50, r 5%, T 1y, dividend 2 paid at 6 months?
d1-05-products-010.back:
$F = S(1+rT) - D(1 + r\,(T - t_D))$.
$F = 50 \times 1.05 - 2 \times 1.025 = 52.50 - 2.05 = 50.45$.
Intuition: you pay financing on the stock and do not get the dividend.

d1-05-products-011.front: Futures fair value with continuous yield, and the intuition.
d1-05-products-011.back:
$F = S\,e^{(r-q)T}$.
Owning the basket costs financing $r$ and pays dividends $q$. The future must match that carry, or arbitrage closes the gap.

d1-05-products-012.front: Index 5000, dividends 20 points (future value), 3-month future 5050. Implied financing (simple)? Your funding is 5.3%. Trade?
d1-05-products-012.back:
$r = \dfrac{(F + D)/S - 1}{T} = \dfrac{5070/5000 - 1}{0.25} = 5.6\%$.
Future is rich by 30 bp a year: buy basket, sell future (cash-and-carry), if 30 bp beats costs.

d1-05-products-013.front: What does a futures roll price?
d1-05-products-013.back:
The calendar spread between the front and next contract.
It prices financing minus dividends for the next period. Rich rolls mean the market pays up for synthetic long exposure.

d1-05-products-014.front: What is a total return future (TRF)?
d1-05-products-014.back:
A listed future whose traded price is the financing spread over a benchmark rate (e.g. Eurex TRFs, CME AIR TRFs).
A cleared alternative to an index TRS: less counterparty capital, and a visible market price for financing.

d1-05-products-015.front: What is an EFP (exchange for physical)?
d1-05-products-015.back:
An agreed swap of a futures position for the underlying basket (or the reverse), at a negotiated basis.
Used to switch between futures and physical without market risk.

d1-05-products-016.front: Client unwinds a 1y swap after 3 months. Why can the desk charge breakage?
d1-05-products-016.back:
The desk may have locked term funding or a term borrow for the full tenor.
Early unwind leaves that cost unhedged. Confirms often set unwind fees or minimum terms.

d1-06-desk-map-001.front: What do cash equities (high touch / low touch) desks do?
d1-06-desk-map-001.back:
Execute client orders in stocks: high touch with sales traders, low touch via algos and DMA.
Mostly agency; risk on the book is small.
d1-06-desk-map-001.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-002.front: What is a risk bid from a program trading desk?
d1-06-desk-map-002.back:
The desk buys or sells a whole client basket at a guaranteed price (e.g. the close minus a discount).
The desk takes the basket onto its book and unwinds the risk afterwards.
d1-06-desk-map-002.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-003.front: What does a Delta One desk run?
d1-06-desk-map-003.back:
Client swaps (single stock, index, custom baskets), futures and index arbitrage, ETFs, financing and dividends.
It hedges with internalization, physical stock, dealer swaps, futures and options.
d1-06-desk-map-003.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-004.front: What does prime brokerage provide to hedge funds?
d1-06-desk-map-004.back:
Financing of longs (margin loans), stock borrow for shorts, custody, clearing and reporting.
Synthetic prime (portfolio swaps) overlaps with Delta One.
d1-06-desk-map-004.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-005.front: What does a stock loan / sec lending desk do?
d1-06-desk-map-005.back:
Sources borrow from agent lenders (custodians lending for pension funds and asset managers) and from internal inventory.
Lends to clients and internal desks that are short. Manages fees, recalls and collateral.
d1-06-desk-map-005.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-006.front: Why does a bank run firm-wide inventory management?
d1-06-desk-map-006.back:
To match internal longs (desk hedges, PB margin collateral) with internal shorts before borrowing outside.
Internal sourcing is cheaper and frees balance sheet.
d1-06-desk-map-006.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-007.front: What is rehypothecation in prime brokerage?
d1-06-desk-map-007.back:
The PB reuses the client's margin securities, e.g. lends them or repos them.
US rules (SEC 15c3-3) limit reuse to 140% of the client's debit balance.
d1-06-desk-map-007.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-008.front: What does a flow vol desk do, and how does it touch Delta One?
d1-06-desk-map-008.back:
Makes markets in vanilla options (listed and OTC) and runs vol, skew and term-structure risk.
It needs delta hedges, borrow costs and dividend forecasts: inputs Delta One prices.
d1-06-desk-map-008.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-009.front: What does an exotics / structured products desk do?
d1-06-desk-map-009.back:
Designs and hedges notes and exotic options (e.g. autocallables).
It carries long-dated vol, dividend and correlation risk.
d1-06-desk-map-009.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-010.front: Why is a structured note a funding source for the bank?
d1-06-desk-map-010.back:
The investor pays cash upfront and the bank repays at maturity. Economically it is bank borrowing.
The investor takes the bank's credit risk. Issuance spreads are often cheaper than plain unsecured debt.
d1-06-desk-map-010.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-011.front: How do structured notes and Delta One complement each other inside a bank?
d1-06-desk-map-011.back:
Notes bring cash in (funding provider). Delta One inventory needs cash (funding consumer).
Treasury nets them internally and credits or charges each desk through FTP.
d1-06-desk-map-011.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-012.back: Funding and liquidity: issuance, repo strategy, liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR) and the internal FTP curve.
d1-06-desk-map-012.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-013.front: What does an XVA desk do?
d1-06-desk-map-013.back: Prices and hedges valuation adjustments on derivatives (CVA, FVA, KVA, MVA) and charges them to trading desks.
d1-06-desk-map-013.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-014.front: What do strats do on a trading desk?
d1-06-desk-map-014.back:
Build the desk's models, pricing and risk tools, and software; analyse flows and P&L.
They sit with traders, not in a separate research unit.
d1-06-desk-map-014.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

d1-06-desk-map-015.front: Who controls a trading desk's P&L and risk independently?
d1-06-desk-map-015.back: Product control (P&L, valuation, price verification) and market risk management (limits, VaR, stress).
d1-06-desk-map-015.source: Learn Anything — Delta One prep (2026); generic bulge-bracket structure

llm-01-transformers-001.front: Which two RNN problems does self-attention remove?
llm-01-transformers-001.back:
1. Long-range links fade: information crosses many steps. With attention, every token reads every other token in one step.
2. No parallel training: step $t$ waits for step $t-1$. With attention, all positions are computed at once.

llm-01-transformers-002.front: Write scaled dot-product attention, and read it in one sentence.
llm-01-transformers-002.back:
$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$
Score every token by query·key, turn each row of scores into weights, and average the values with those weights.

llm-01-transformers-003.front: Attention: what are the query, the key and the value of a token?
llm-01-transformers-003.back:
**Query**: what this token looks for.
**Key**: what a token offers for matching.
**Value**: the content passed on when matched.

llm-01-transformers-004.back:
With unit-variance entries, $q \cdot k$ has variance $d_k$.
Large scores saturate the softmax: one weight near 1, tiny gradients. Scaling restores unit variance.

llm-01-transformers-005.front: What is the causal mask, and how is it applied?
llm-01-transformers-005.back:
In a decoder, token $t$ must not see tokens after $t$.
Scores for future positions are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so their weights are 0.

llm-01-transformers-006.back:
Each head works in a smaller subspace ($d/h$; e.g. $768/12 = 64$) and can learn a different relation (syntax, coreference, position).
Outputs are concatenated and projected back to $d$. Total cost is about that of one big head.

llm-01-transformers-007.front: Time and memory cost of full attention over $n$ tokens.
llm-01-transformers-007.back:
Time $O(n^2 d)$; the score matrix is $n \times n$ per head.
Doubling the context roughly quadruples attention cost.

llm-01-transformers-008.back:
It computes **exact** attention in tiles held in fast on-chip memory, never storing the full $n \times n$ matrix.
Fewer memory reads and writes: faster, and memory linear in $n$. Same result.

llm-01-transformers-009.front: Why does a transformer need positional information?
llm-01-transformers-009.back:
Attention alone ignores order: shuffle the input tokens and you get the same outputs, shuffled.
So position must be injected, e.g. RoPE on $q$ and $k$, or a position vector added to the embeddings.

llm-01-transformers-010.front: The two sublayers of a transformer block, and what each one does.
llm-01-transformers-010.back:
1. **Self-attention**: tokens exchange information.
2. **MLP**: each token is processed alone.
Each one is wrapped as $x \leftarrow x + f(\text{norm}(x))$.
llm-01-transformers-010.source: Vaswani et al. 2017; pre-norm as in GPT-2

llm-01-transformers-011.back:
The vector per token that every layer reads from and adds to.
Layers write increments, not replacements. This keeps gradients flowing in deep stacks.

llm-01-transformers-012.back:
Start from bytes or characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
Result: common words are one token, rare words split into subwords. English averages about 4 characters per token.
llm-01-transformers-012.source: Sennrich et al. 2016 (BPE); OpenAI tokenizer rule of thumb

llm-01-transformers-013.front: How does a decoder turn the last hidden state into a next token?
llm-01-transformers-013.back:
Final norm, then unembedding: hidden state $(d)$ × output matrix $(d, \text{vocab})$ → one logit per vocabulary token.
Softmax gives probabilities; a sampler picks the token.

llm-01-transformers-014.front: Training objective of a decoder LLM.
llm-01-transformers-014.back:
Minimize the cross-entropy of the next token:
$L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_t \ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$
Per position: minus the log of the probability given to the correct token.

llm-01-transformers-015.front: What is the KV cache, and why is it valid in a decoder?
llm-01-transformers-015.back:
During generation, the keys and values of past tokens are stored, not recomputed. Each new token computes only its own $q, k, v$ and attends to the cache.
Valid because of the causal mask: a past token never sees later tokens, so its $k$ and $v$ never change.

llm-01-transformers-016.front: KV cache size: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, 8,192 tokens, fp16.
llm-01-transformers-016.back:
$2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 8192 \times 2$ bytes $\approx 1$ GiB per sequence.
(2 for K and V; last 2 is bytes per value.)

llm-01-transformers-017.front: Prefill vs decode: what limits each?
llm-01-transformers-017.back:
**Prefill** processes the whole prompt in parallel: compute-bound.
**Decode** produces one token at a time and rereads weights and cache: memory-bandwidth-bound.

llm-01-transformers-018.front: What do multi-query and grouped-query attention (MQA, GQA) save?
llm-01-transformers-018.back:
Several query heads share one set of K and V heads.
The KV cache shrinks by that factor (32 query heads on 8 KV heads → 4× smaller), with a small quality cost.

llm-01-transformers-019.front: What does temperature do in sampling?
llm-01-transformers-019.back:
Divides the logits by $T$ before the softmax.
$T < 1$ sharpens (more deterministic); $T > 1$ flattens (more diverse). $T \to 0$ is greedy: always the top token.

llm-01-transformers-020.back:
Sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least $p$.
It cuts the long tail of unlikely tokens.

llm-01-transformers-021.front: Is generation at temperature 0 fully deterministic?
llm-01-transformers-021.back: Not guaranteed. Batching and non-deterministic GPU kernels can change floating-point sums and flip near-tied tokens.

llm-01-transformers-022.back:
Many MLP "experts"; a router sends each token to the top-k of them.
Total parameters are large, but compute per token uses only the active experts.

llm-01-transformers-023.back:
Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional, for classification and embeddings.
Decoder-only (GPT-style): causal, for generation.
Encoder-decoder (T5): encode input, decode output, e.g. translation.
llm-01-transformers-023.source: Vaswani et al. 2017; Devlin et al. 2019 (BERT); Raffel et al. 2020 (T5)

llm-01-transformers-024.front: What is the "lost in the middle" effect?
llm-01-transformers-024.back:
Models use information at the start and end of a long context better than information in the middle.
Put key instructions and facts at the edges.

llm-02-training-001.front: What does pretraining teach a model?
llm-02-training-001.back:
Next-token prediction over a very large corpus.
The model learns language, facts and patterns, but not yet how to follow instructions.
llm-02-training-001.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-002.front: What do neural scaling laws say?
llm-02-training-002.back:
Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute.
Gains are predictable but diminish: each fixed loss drop needs a multiple of compute.
llm-02-training-002.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-003.front: Chinchilla rule of thumb for compute-optimal training.
llm-02-training-003.back:
About 20 training tokens per parameter; scale data and parameters together.
Example: 70B parameters → 1.4T tokens. Many models now train far beyond this to make inference cheaper.
llm-02-training-003.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-004.front: Approximate training compute for $N$ parameters and $D$ tokens.
llm-02-training-004.back:
$C \approx 6ND$ FLOPs (2 forward + 4 backward per parameter per token).
70B × 1.4T → about $5.9 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs.
llm-02-training-004.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-005.back:
Train on demonstrations: prompt → ideal response.
It teaches format and instruction following.
llm-02-training-005.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-006.back:
1. Humans compare pairs of responses.
2. A reward model learns those preferences.
3. The policy is optimized with RL (e.g. PPO) to maximize reward, with a KL penalty to a reference model.
llm-02-training-006.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-007.front: Why the KL penalty in RLHF?
llm-02-training-007.back:
It keeps the policy close to the reference model.
Without it, the policy drifts and exploits reward-model flaws (reward hacking).
llm-02-training-007.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-008.front: What does DPO change versus RLHF?
llm-02-training-008.back:
It optimizes on preference pairs directly with a classification-style loss.
No separate reward model and no RL loop; simpler and more stable.
llm-02-training-008.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-009.front: What is RL with verifiable rewards?
llm-02-training-009.back:
RL on tasks whose answers can be checked automatically (math answers, code tests).
The checker is the reward. It is central to training reasoning models.
llm-02-training-009.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-010.front: What is LoRA, and how many parameters does it train for a 4096×4096 matrix at rank 8?
llm-02-training-010.back:
Freeze $W$ and learn a low-rank update $\Delta W = BA$, with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times d}$.
$2 \times 4096 \times 8 = 65{,}536$ parameters, vs 16.8M for the full matrix.
llm-02-training-010.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-011.back:
Weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits, e.g. 8 or 4.
Less memory and faster inference, for a small quality loss.
llm-02-training-011.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-012.back:
Train a small student model to match a large teacher's outputs or probabilities.
The student keeps much of the quality at lower cost.
llm-02-training-012.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-013.back:
Training rewards plausible continuations, not calibrated "I don't know".
Mitigations: grounding with retrieval, citations, tools, and training to abstain.
llm-02-training-013.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-02-training-014.front: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning: when to use each?
llm-02-training-014.back:
Prompting first: cheap, fast to change.
RAG: knowledge that changes or is private.
Fine-tuning: stable behavior, style or format at scale; not for fresh facts.
llm-02-training-014.source: Standard LLM practice; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA)

llm-03-agents-001.back: An LLM in a loop: it chooses an action (often a tool call), reads the result, and repeats until the goal is met.

llm-03-agents-002.front: Workflow vs agent: who decides the path?
llm-03-agents-002.back:
**Workflow**: code fixes the path; the LLM fills steps.
**Agent**: the LLM decides the path at run time.
Start with the simplest that works; agents cost more and fail in more ways.

llm-03-agents-003.front: How does tool calling work mechanically?
llm-03-agents-003.back:
The app describes each tool by name, description and JSON schema.
The model outputs a structured call; the app runs it and returns the result; the model continues.
The model never executes anything itself.

llm-03-agents-004.back:
A loop that interleaves reasoning ("thought") and actions (tool calls), with each observation fed back before the next thought.
It is the pattern behind most tool-using agents.

llm-03-agents-005.front: Per-step success 95%, 10 dependent steps. Chance the whole run succeeds?
llm-03-agents-005.back:
$0.95^{10} \approx 60\%$.
Errors compound: shorten the chain, and add checks, retries and human review.

llm-03-agents-006.back:
Choosing what enters the context window at each step: instructions, tools, retrieved data, history.
Context is finite and attention dilutes; curate, summarize and isolate.
llm-03-agents-006.source: Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (2025)

llm-03-agents-007.back:
Instructions hidden in untrusted data (a web page, email, file or tool output) that hijack the agent.
The model cannot reliably tell data from instructions.
llm-03-agents-007.source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications; Simon Willison

llm-03-agents-008.front: What is the "lethal trifecta" for agent security?
llm-03-agents-008.back:
1. Access to private data.
2. Exposure to untrusted content.
3. A way to send data out.
All three together let an injection exfiltrate data. Remove at least one.

llm-03-agents-009.back: Treat tool outputs as data; least-privilege tools; human approval for side effects; separate untrusted content from privileged actions; allow-lists for destinations.
llm-03-agents-009.source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications; Simon Willison

llm-03-agents-010.back: Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve relevant chunks, put them in the context, and answer from them with citations.

llm-03-agents-011.back:
Vectors where semantic similarity ≈ cosine similarity.
Query and documents use the same model; search finds nearest neighbours.

llm-03-agents-012.back:
Small chunks: precise matches, but lose context.
Large chunks: more context, but noisier matches and more tokens. Overlap and structure-aware splits help.

llm-03-agents-013.front: What is hybrid search in RAG?
llm-03-agents-013.back:
Run keyword search (BM25) and vector search together, then merge the two rankings.
Keywords catch exact terms (tickers, codes, names); vectors catch meaning.

llm-03-agents-014.front: How do you evaluate an LLM feature?
llm-03-agents-014.back:
A fixed test set with graders: exact or code checks where possible, LLM-as-judge for open text, human labels to calibrate.
Run it on every prompt or model change, like regression tests.

llm-03-agents-015.back:
Position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference.
Mitigate: swap order, use rubrics, calibrate against human labels.

llm-03-agents-016.back:
Force the response into a JSON schema so code can parse it.
Still validate: schema-valid is not the same as correct.

llm-03-agents-017.front: Short-term vs long-term memory for agents.
llm-03-agents-017.back:
Short-term: state of one conversation or thread.
Long-term: facts kept across sessions in a store, retrieved when relevant.

llm-03-agents-018.front: When is a multi-agent (orchestrator–workers) design worth it?
llm-03-agents-018.back:
When subtasks are independent and context-heavy: workers get clean contexts and run in parallel.
Cost: many more tokens and harder debugging.

llm-03-agents-019.front: Why should agent tools be idempotent?
llm-03-agents-019.back:
Agents and frameworks retry and resume. A retried non-idempotent tool can act twice (two orders, two emails).
Use idempotency keys or check-then-act.

llm-03-agents-020.front: What is prompt caching, and how do you design for it?
llm-03-agents-020.back:
The provider reuses computation for an identical prompt prefix.
Put stable content (system prompt, tools, documents) first and changing content last.

llm-03-agents-021.back:
An open protocol to connect LLM apps to tools and data.
Each tool is built once as an MCP server and works with any MCP client: N + M integrations instead of N × M.

llm-03-agents-022.back:
**Host**: the LLM app (e.g. a chat app or IDE).
**Client**: the connector inside the host, one per server.
**Server**: exposes tools, resources and prompts.

llm-03-agents-023.front: The three MCP server primitives and who controls each.
llm-03-agents-023.back:
**Tools**: actions; model-controlled.
**Resources**: data for context; application-controlled.
**Prompts**: templates; user-controlled.

llm-03-agents-024.back:
stdio for local servers; Streamable HTTP for remote servers.
Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0.

llm-04-langgraph-001.back:
An agent or workflow as a graph: nodes are functions over a shared state; edges decide what runs next, including cycles.
Low-level orchestration with persistence built in.

llm-04-langgraph-002.front: What is a StateGraph's state, and what does a node return?
llm-04-langgraph-002.back:
A typed schema (TypedDict, Pydantic model or dataclass).
A node receives the state and returns a **partial update**, not the whole state.

llm-04-langgraph-003.front: What is a reducer, and what is the default?
llm-04-langgraph-003.back:
The function that merges a node's update into a state key.
Default: overwrite. `Annotated[list, operator.add]` appends; `add_messages` appends messages and updates by id.

llm-04-langgraph-004.back:
`add_edge(a, b)`: b always runs after a.
`add_conditional_edges(a, router)`: a routing function reads the state and returns the next node(s). `START` and `END` mark entry and exit.

llm-04-langgraph-005.back: Validates the graph and returns a runnable. The checkpointer (and store) attach here.

llm-04-langgraph-006.back:
Saves a state snapshot at each super-step, keyed by `thread_id` in the config.
It enables conversation memory, resume after failure, human-in-the-loop and time travel. `InMemorySaver` for tests; Postgres or similar for production.

llm-04-langgraph-007.back:
Checkpointer: state of one thread (short-term memory).
Store: key–value memory shared across threads (long-term memory, e.g. user preferences).

llm-04-langgraph-008.back:
LangGraph runs in Pregel-style steps. Nodes scheduled together run in parallel in one step.
Their updates apply at the end of the step through the reducers.

llm-04-langgraph-009.front: Two parallel nodes write the same key in one super-step, with no reducer. What happens?
llm-04-langgraph-009.back:
An `InvalidUpdateError`: LangGraph cannot choose between two overwrites.
Fix: add a reducer for that key, or write to different keys.

llm-04-langgraph-010.front: How does `interrupt()` work, and what is the main pitfall?
llm-04-langgraph-010.back:
It pauses the graph inside a node and surfaces a value (e.g. for human approval). It needs a checkpointer and a `thread_id`. Resume with `Command(resume=...)`; that value becomes the return of `interrupt()`.
Pitfall: the node **re-runs from its start**, so side effects before the interrupt run again.

llm-04-langgraph-011.front: What does returning a `Command` from a node do?
llm-04-langgraph-011.back:
It combines a state update and routing: `Command(update={...}, goto="node")`.
