Routing lives in the node instead of a separate conditional edge.

llm-04-langgraph-012.back:
Dynamic fan-out (map-reduce): a router returns `Send("node", substate)` for each item.
Each branch gets its own input; a reducer gathers results.

llm-04-langgraph-013.front: Two ways to use a subgraph.
llm-04-langgraph-013.back:
1. Add the compiled subgraph directly as a node: parent and child share state keys.
2. Call it from a wrapper node that maps parent state in and out: different schemas.

llm-04-langgraph-014.back:
`values`: full state after each step.
`updates`: only each node's update.
`messages`: LLM tokens as they generate.
`custom`: data a node emits itself.

llm-04-langgraph-015.front: What is time travel in LangGraph?
llm-04-langgraph-015.back:
List a thread's checkpoints (`get_state_history`, newest first), then replay from one, or fork from it with `update_state`.
You can only resume from a super-step boundary. Useful for debugging and "what if" reruns.

llm-04-langgraph-016.front: What is durable execution, and how do you avoid repeating side effects on resume?
llm-04-langgraph-016.back:
A run resumes from its last checkpoint after a crash or pause.
Wrap side effects in tasks or make them idempotent, so a resumed run does not repeat them.

llm-04-langgraph-017.front: What protects a cyclic graph from looping forever?
llm-04-langgraph-017.back:
The recursion limit: a cap on **super-steps** per run, set as `recursion_limit` at the top level of the config (not inside `configurable`).
Exceeding it raises `GraphRecursionError`. Also design explicit exit conditions.

sd-01-scale-001.back:
Latency: time for one request.
Throughput: requests completed per unit time. Batching often raises throughput and latency together.

sd-01-scale-002.front: Why watch p99 instead of the average latency?
sd-01-scale-002.back:
Averages hide the slow tail that real users hit.
A page that calls many services waits for the slowest one, so tail latency dominates.

sd-01-scale-003.front: A request fans out to 100 servers. Each is slow 1% of the time. Chance the request is slow?
sd-01-scale-003.back:
$1 - 0.99^{100} \approx 63\%$.
Fan-out turns rare tail events into the common case.

sd-01-scale-004.front: State Little's law and use it: 2,000 req/s, 50 ms each.
sd-01-scale-004.back:
$L = \lambda W$: items in the system = arrival rate × time in system.
$2000 \times 0.05 = 100$ concurrent requests. Size pools and threads from this.

sd-01-scale-005.front: State Amdahl's law. 90% of a job parallelizes, 10 cores: speedup?

sd-01-scale-006.back:
Vertical: a bigger machine; simple, but capped and a single point of failure.
Horizontal: more machines; needs stateless services or partitioned data.

sd-01-scale-007.back:
Any instance can serve any request, so you add instances behind a load balancer.
State moves to a database, cache or token.

sd-01-scale-008.back:
L4 routes by IP and port (fast, protocol-agnostic).
L7 reads HTTP: routes by path or header, terminates TLS, retries.

sd-01-scale-009.back:
**Cache-aside**: app reads cache, on miss loads DB and fills cache.
**Write-through**: write cache and DB together; consistent, slower writes.
**Write-back**: write cache, flush to DB later; fast, risk of loss.

sd-01-scale-010.front: What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
sd-01-scale-010.back:
A hot key expires and many requests hit the database at once.
Fixes: request coalescing (one loader), jittered TTLs, refresh before expiry.

sd-01-scale-011.back:
When the cache is full, it removes the least recently used item.
Usual build: hash map + doubly linked list, O(1) get and put.

sd-01-scale-012.back: L1 cache ~1 ns; main memory ~100 ns; SSD random read ~100 µs; same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms; cross-continent round trip ~100–150 ms.

sd-01-scale-013.front: How does a token bucket rate limiter work?
sd-01-scale-013.back:
A bucket holds up to $b$ tokens and refills at rate $r$. Each request takes a token or is rejected.
Allows bursts up to $b$ and an average rate $r$.

sd-01-scale-014.back:
A slow consumer signals producers to slow down (bounded queues, blocking, credits) instead of buffering without limit.
It prevents memory blow-ups and cascading failure.

sd-01-scale-015.front: Why consistent hashing? Compare with hash mod n when you add a node.
sd-01-scale-015.back:
Hash mod n: adding a node remaps almost all keys.
Consistent hashing: keys and nodes sit on a ring; adding a node moves only about $1/n$ of keys. Virtual nodes even out the load.

sd-02-data-001.back: During a network partition, a distributed store must choose consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (serve possibly stale data).
sd-02-data-001.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-002.front: What does PACELC add to CAP?
sd-02-data-002.back: Else (no partition), there is still a trade-off between latency and consistency.
sd-02-data-002.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-003.front: Strong vs eventual consistency; what is read-your-writes?
sd-02-data-003.back:
Strong: every read sees the latest write.
Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop.
Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own writes, even if others see them later.
sd-02-data-003.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-004.front: Leader–follower replication: benefit and main issue.
sd-02-data-004.back:
Writes go to the leader; followers copy them and serve reads, so reads scale.
Issue: replication lag gives stale reads from followers.
sd-02-data-004.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-005.back:
Sync: the write waits for the replica; no data loss on failover, higher latency.
Async: fast writes; a leader crash can lose recent writes.
sd-02-data-005.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-006.front: Quorum rule for reads to see the latest write. Example with N = 3.
sd-02-data-006.back:
$R + W > N$: every read set overlaps every write set.
N = 3, W = 2, R = 2: $4 > 3$.
sd-02-data-006.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-007.back:
Range: efficient range scans, but hot spots (e.g. all writes on today's date).
Hash: even load, but range queries hit all partitions.
sd-02-data-007.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-008.back:
B-tree: updates pages in place; fast reads; classic in relational DBs.
LSM-tree: append to memory, flush sorted files, compact later; fast writes, reads may check several files.
sd-02-data-008.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-009.back: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (invariants hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
sd-02-data-009.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-010.front: What is write skew, and which isolation level allows it?
sd-02-data-010.back:
Two transactions read the same data, each writes a different row, and together they break an invariant (e.g. both on-call doctors go off duty).
Snapshot isolation allows it; serializable prevents it.
sd-02-data-010.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-011.back:
Pessimistic: lock before writing; others wait.
Optimistic: write with a version check; retry on conflict. Good when conflicts are rare.
sd-02-data-011.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-012.front: Why columnar storage for analytics and market data?
sd-02-data-012.back:
Queries read few columns over many rows. Columns store contiguously and compress well.
Examples: Parquet, kdb+, ClickHouse.
sd-02-data-012.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-013.back:
Store every change as an immutable event; current state = fold of the events.
Gives a full audit trail and replay. Cost: snapshots and schema evolution of events.
sd-02-data-013.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-014.back:
Separate the write model (commands) from read models (queries), each shaped for its job.
Read models are often built from events and are eventually consistent.
sd-02-data-014.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-02-data-015.back:
Normalize: each fact once; consistent writes, more joins.
Denormalize: duplicate data for fast reads; writes must update every copy.
sd-02-data-015.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; standard practice

sd-03-reliability-001.front: What is idempotency, and how do you get it for a POST?
sd-03-reliability-001.back:
Repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once.
For POST: the client sends an idempotency key; the server stores the result per key and returns it on repeats.

sd-03-reliability-002.front: Why exponential backoff with jitter on retries?
sd-03-reliability-002.back:
Backoff gives the failing service time to recover.
Jitter spreads retries in time, so clients do not retry in synchronized waves.

sd-03-reliability-003.front: What does a circuit breaker do?
sd-03-reliability-003.back:
After repeated failures it stops calling the dependency and fails fast.
After a pause it lets a few test calls through (half-open) and closes again on success.

sd-03-reliability-004.front: Why must every network call have a timeout?
sd-03-reliability-004.back:
Without one, a hung dependency holds threads and connections forever and the failure spreads.
Propagate deadlines so downstream calls stop when the caller has given up.

sd-03-reliability-005.back:
At-most-once: may lose messages.
At-least-once: may duplicate them.
"Exactly-once" in practice = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing.

sd-03-reliability-006.back:
Queue: a message is removed once acknowledged.
Log: messages are retained; each consumer tracks its offset and can replay.

sd-03-reliability-007.back: Only within a partition. Pick the key so events that must stay ordered (e.g. one account) share a partition.

sd-03-reliability-008.front: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
sd-03-reliability-008.back:
Write the state change and an outbox row in the same DB transaction; a relay publishes outbox rows to the broker.
No lost or phantom events between DB and broker.

sd-03-reliability-009.back:
A long business transaction split into local transactions, each with a compensating action.
On failure, run compensations in reverse instead of a distributed lock.

sd-03-reliability-010.back:
Where messages go after repeated processing failures.
It stops one poison message from blocking the stream; inspect and replay later.

sd-03-reliability-011.back:
Liveness: is the process alive? Fail → restart it.
Readiness: can it serve traffic now? Fail → remove from the load balancer, do not restart.

sd-03-reliability-012.back: Isolate resources (thread pools, connections) per dependency or feature, so one failure cannot exhaust everything.

sd-03-reliability-013.front: Logs, metrics, traces: what does each answer?
sd-03-reliability-013.back:
Metrics: is something wrong, and how much?
Traces: where in the request path?
Logs: what exactly happened in that component?

sd-03-reliability-014.back:
SLI: a measured indicator (e.g. % requests under 300 ms).
SLO: the internal target (99.9%).
SLA: the contractual promise, with penalties.
Error budget: 1 − SLO; spend it on releases, freeze when it runs out.

sd-03-reliability-015.back:
Blue-green: run the new version alongside, switch all traffic at once, switch back to roll back.
Canary: send a small share of traffic first, watch metrics, then widen.

sd-04-web-security-001.front: Which HTTP methods are safe, and which are idempotent?
sd-04-web-security-001.back:
Safe (no state change): GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.
Idempotent: the safe ones + PUT and DELETE.
POST and PATCH are not idempotent by default.
sd-04-web-security-001.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-002.back:
401: not authenticated (no or invalid credentials).
403: authenticated, but not allowed.
sd-04-web-security-002.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-003.back:
HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read the cookie (limits XSS theft).
Secure: sent only over HTTPS.
SameSite (Lax/Strict): not sent on most cross-site requests (limits CSRF).
sd-04-web-security-003.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-004.front: What does CORS do, and what does it not do?
sd-04-web-security-004.back:
The browser blocks cross-origin reads unless the server allows the origin (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`); non-simple requests send an OPTIONS preflight first.
It is not server-side protection: curl or a server ignores it.
sd-04-web-security-004.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-005.front: What is CSRF, and its main defences?
sd-04-web-security-005.back:
A malicious site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request (cookies attach automatically).
Defences: SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, checking Origin.
sd-04-web-security-005.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-006.front: What is XSS, and its main defences?
sd-04-web-security-006.back:
Attacker script runs inside your origin and acts as the user.
Defences: output encoding, avoid raw HTML injection, Content Security Policy, HttpOnly cookies.
sd-04-web-security-006.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-007.front: Server session vs bearer token (e.g. JWT).
sd-04-web-security-007.back:
Session: random id in a cookie, state on the server; easy to revoke.
Self-contained token: no lookup per request; hard to revoke before expiry, so keep lifetimes short.
sd-04-web-security-007.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-008.front: Structure of a JWT, and what to verify.
sd-04-web-security-008.back:
`header.payload.signature`, base64url. Signed, **not encrypted**: anyone can read the payload.
Verify signature, `exp`, `iss` and `aud`.
sd-04-web-security-008.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-009.back:
OAuth 2.0: delegated **authorization**: an access token to call an API.
OIDC: an identity layer on top for **authentication**: an ID token that says who the user is.
sd-04-web-security-009.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-010.front: Key claims in an OIDC ID token.
sd-04-web-security-010.back: `iss` (issuer), `sub` (user id at the issuer), `aud` (your client id), `exp`, `iat`, and `nonce` (binds the token to your request).
sd-04-web-security-010.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-011.front: Steps of the authorization code flow.
sd-04-web-security-011.back:
1. App redirects the user to the IdP with client id, scopes, redirect URI, `state`.
2. User signs in; IdP redirects back with a short-lived code.
3. App's backend exchanges the code for tokens.
4. App verifies the ID token and starts a session.
sd-04-web-security-011.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-012.front: What does PKCE add, and how?
sd-04-web-security-012.back:
Stops a stolen authorization code from being redeemed.
App creates a random `code_verifier`, sends `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))` at login, and the verifier at token exchange.
sd-04-web-security-012.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-013.back:
`state`: ties the redirect back to the request that started it (CSRF on the callback).
`nonce`: ties the ID token to that request (replay).
sd-04-web-security-013.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-014.back:
Access token: short-lived, sent to APIs.
Refresh token: longer-lived, kept by the client or backend, exchanged for new access tokens. Protect it more.
sd-04-web-security-014.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-015.front: How does an app verify ID tokens without sharing a secret with the IdP?
sd-04-web-security-015.back: It reads the IdP's discovery document (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`), fetches the public keys (JWKS), and checks the signature.
sd-04-web-security-015.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-016.back:
One login at an identity provider gives access to many apps that trust it.
Protocols: SAML (older, enterprise) and OIDC.
sd-04-web-security-016.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-017.back:
Confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication by certificate.
Ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) gives forward secrecy: a later key leak does not decrypt past traffic.
sd-04-web-security-017.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-04-web-security-018.front: Where should a browser app keep OAuth tokens?
sd-04-web-security-018.back:
Not in localStorage: any XSS can read it.
Prefer a backend-for-frontend: the server holds tokens; the browser gets an HttpOnly session cookie.
sd-04-web-security-018.source: RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OWASP

sd-05-web-apps-001.front: CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR.
sd-05-web-apps-001.back:
CSR: the browser renders from JS.
SSR: the server renders HTML per request.
SSG: HTML built at build time.
ISR: static pages regenerated in the background after a set time.
sd-05-web-apps-001.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-002.back:
The browser attaches React's event handlers to server-rendered HTML, making it interactive.
A mismatch between server and client output causes hydration errors.
sd-05-web-apps-002.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-003.front: React Server Components vs Client Components.
sd-05-web-apps-003.back:
Server Components render on the server, ship no JS, and can read databases and secrets directly; no state or effects.
Client Components (`"use client"`) run in the browser for interactivity.
sd-05-web-apps-003.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-004.front: What reaches the browser in a Next.js app, and what must not?
sd-05-web-apps-004.back:
Everything in client components and env vars prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is public.
Secrets and tokens stay in server-only code.
sd-05-web-apps-004.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-005.front: What is a route handler in the Next.js App Router?
sd-05-web-apps-005.back:
A file `app/.../route.ts` that exports `GET`, `POST`, etc.
It is a backend endpoint inside the Next.js app.
sd-05-web-apps-005.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-006.front: Why must a Server Action check authorization itself?
sd-05-web-apps-006.back:
A Server Action is a public HTTP endpoint, even if only your form calls it.
Anyone can call it directly, so authenticate and authorize inside it.
sd-05-web-apps-006.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-007.front: Backend-for-frontend (BFF) for an agent UI: what goes where?
sd-05-web-apps-007.back:
Browser ↔ Next.js server (session cookie) ↔ agent backend (e.g. LangGraph) and APIs (tokens).
Tokens and tool credentials never reach the browser.
sd-05-web-apps-007.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-05-web-apps-008.front: SSE vs WebSocket for streaming LLM output.
sd-05-web-apps-008.back:
SSE: one-way server → client over plain HTTP, auto-reconnect; enough for token streaming.
WebSocket: two-way, persistent; for real-time interaction both ways.
sd-05-web-apps-008.source: Next.js and React documentation; standard practice

sd-06-trading-systems-001.back:
OMS: order lifecycle, allocations, compliance, positions (portfolio side).
EMS: execution: routing, algos, market access.

sd-06-trading-systems-002.front: What is FIX? Name the new-order and execution-report message types.
sd-06-trading-systems-002.back:
A tag=value messaging standard for orders and executions.
NewOrderSingle is `35=D`; ExecutionReport is `35=8`.

sd-06-trading-systems-003.front: Which pre-trade risk checks must sit before market access?
sd-06-trading-systems-003.back:
Fat-finger (price and size), credit and position limits, restricted lists, duplicate-order checks.
In the US, the SEC market access rule (15c3-5) requires them.

sd-06-trading-systems-004.front: Snapshot vs incremental market data, and gap handling.
sd-06-trading-systems-004.back:
Snapshot: the full book. Incremental: changes with sequence numbers.
On a sequence gap, stop applying updates, request a snapshot or replay, then resume.

sd-06-trading-systems-005.front: What is conflation in market data distribution?
sd-06-trading-systems-005.back:
For slow consumers, send only the latest state per instrument instead of every tick.
Keeps them current instead of falling behind.

sd-06-trading-systems-006.front: Why build position keeping on event sourcing?
sd-06-trading-systems-006.back: Positions = fold of fills and corrections. Full audit trail, replay to any time, and easy reconciliation.

sd-06-trading-systems-007.front: Decompose a day's P&L for a Delta One book.
sd-06-trading-systems-007.back:
1. Position P&L: start-of-day position × price move.
2. New-trade P&L: new trades vs end-of-day mark.
3. Carry: financing and dividends accrued.
4. Fees and other adjustments.
Unexplained remainder = a break to investigate.

sd-06-trading-systems-008.back:
Matching positions and cash across front-office systems, books and records, and custodians or clearers.
Differences ("breaks") get investigated and fixed daily.

sd-06-trading-systems-009.front: Why record and replay market data in trading systems?
sd-06-trading-systems-009.back: Deterministic replays reproduce bugs and test strategy or pricing changes against real sequences.

sd-04-web-security-019.front: SSO: what do the IdP and the SP (relying party) each do?
sd-04-web-security-019.back:
IdP: authenticates the user and issues signed assertions or tokens.
SP / relying party: trusts the IdP's signature and starts its own session. It never sees the password.
sd-04-web-security-019.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-020.front: How does SAML differ from OIDC in practice?
sd-04-web-security-020.back:
SAML: XML assertions, signed, sent through the browser (POST); common for enterprise web SSO.
OIDC: JSON/JWT on top of OAuth 2.0; fits SPAs, mobile and APIs.
sd-04-web-security-020.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-021.front: SP-initiated vs IdP-initiated SSO, and why prefer SP-initiated?
sd-04-web-security-021.back:
SP-initiated: the app sends the user to the IdP with a request it can match on return.
IdP-initiated: the IdP posts an unsolicited assertion; no request to match, so it is easier to inject or replay.
sd-04-web-security-021.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-022.front: After OIDC login, how many sessions exist, and why is logout hard?
sd-04-web-security-022.back:
At least two: the IdP session and each app's own session.
Logging out of one app does not end the IdP session or other apps' sessions. Single logout needs extra protocol work.
sd-04-web-security-022.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-023.front: Which OAuth flow fits machine-to-machine calls?
sd-04-web-security-023.back: Client credentials: the service authenticates as itself (client id + secret or key) and gets an access token. No user involved.
sd-04-web-security-023.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-024.front: Local JWT validation vs token introspection.
sd-04-web-security-024.back:
Local: verify signature and claims with the IdP's public keys; fast, but cannot see revocation before expiry.
Introspection: ask the authorization server if the token is active; current, but a network call per check.
sd-04-web-security-024.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-025.back:
Scopes: what the client app may do on the user's behalf (e.g. `read:positions`).
Roles or claims: what the user is allowed to do. Authorization needs both.
sd-04-web-security-025.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-026.back:
RBAC: permissions attach to roles; users get roles.
ABAC: rules on attributes of user, resource and context (desk, region, time). More expressive, harder to audit.
sd-04-web-security-026.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-04-web-security-027.front: An agent backend must call a downstream API as the signed-in user. What is the clean pattern?
sd-04-web-security-027.back:
Token exchange (RFC 8693, "on-behalf-of"): trade the user's token for a new token scoped to the downstream API.
Do not forward the user's original token everywhere, and do not use a shared service account that hides who acted.
sd-04-web-security-027.source: RFC 6749, RFC 8693, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect Core 1.0

sd-07-crypto-001.front: Hash vs HMAC vs digital signature vs encryption: what does each give?
sd-07-crypto-001.back:
Hash: a fingerprint; detects changes, no key.
HMAC: integrity + authenticity with a **shared** secret key.
Signature: integrity + authenticity with a **private** key; anyone can verify with the public key.
Encryption: confidentiality.

sd-07-crypto-002.back:
$\text{HMAC}(K, m) = H\big((K \oplus \text{opad}) \,\|\, H((K \oplus \text{ipad}) \,\|\, m)\big)$.
Two nested hashes with the key mixed in. Only a key holder can produce or check the tag.

sd-07-crypto-003.front: Why not use $H(\text{key} \,\|\, \text{message})$ as a MAC?
sd-07-crypto-003.back:
With Merkle–Damgård hashes (e.g. SHA-256), an attacker can extend the message and compute a valid tag without the key (length-extension attack).
HMAC's nested construction prevents it.

sd-07-crypto-004.front: Why compare MACs with a constant-time function?
sd-07-crypto-004.back:
A normal comparison stops at the first different byte. Response timing then leaks how many bytes match, and the attacker guesses byte by byte.
Use e.g. Python `hmac.compare_digest`.

sd-07-crypto-005.front: How do you verify a signed webhook?
sd-07-crypto-005.back:
1. Recompute HMAC over the **raw** body (plus the timestamp) with the shared secret.
2. Compare in constant time.
3. Reject if the timestamp is outside a short window (replay).

sd-07-crypto-006.front: HMAC vs digital signature: which gives non-repudiation, and why?
sd-07-crypto-006.back:
The signature. Only the private-key holder can sign.
With HMAC, both parties hold the key, so either could have produced the tag.

sd-07-crypto-007.front: JWT HS256 vs RS256/ES256: when to use which?
sd-07-crypto-007.back:
HS256: HMAC with a shared secret; every verifier can also mint tokens.
RS256/ES256: the issuer signs with a private key; services verify with the public key. Use asymmetric when many services verify.

sd-07-crypto-008.front: What is the JWT algorithm-confusion attack, and the fix?
sd-07-crypto-008.back:
The attacker changes `alg` (to `none`, or from RS256 to HS256 using the public key as the HMAC secret) and the library accepts it.
Fix: pin the expected algorithm and key on the server; never trust `alg` from the token.

sd-07-crypto-009.back:
With a slow, salted, memory-hard function: Argon2id (or bcrypt, scrypt).
Never plain SHA-256: GPUs try billions of guesses per second.

sd-07-crypto-010.front: What does a salt protect against?
sd-07-crypto-010.back:
Precomputed tables and same-password detection. Each user gets a random salt, so identical passwords hash differently.
A salt is not secret.

sd-07-crypto-011.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, and how TLS combines them.
sd-07-crypto-011.back:
Symmetric (AES): one shared key; fast.
Asymmetric: key pairs; slow, but no shared secret needed in advance.
TLS uses asymmetric key exchange to agree a symmetric key, then encrypts data symmetrically.

sd-07-crypto-012.front: What is AEAD, and the one rule never to break?
sd-07-crypto-012.back:
Authenticated encryption (e.g. AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305): confidentiality + integrity in one step.
Never reuse a nonce with the same key: it can reveal plaintext and allow forgeries.

sd-07-crypto-013.back:
A data key encrypts the data; a master key in a KMS encrypts the data key.
Store the encrypted data key with the data. Rotating or revoking the master key controls access without re-encrypting everything.

sd-07-crypto-014.front: What is mTLS, and where is it used?
sd-07-crypto-014.back:
Mutual TLS: the client also presents a certificate, so both sides authenticate.
Common for service-to-service traffic in internal networks and service meshes.

sd-07-crypto-015.front: How does a browser trust a server certificate?
sd-07-crypto-015.back:
The certificate chains through intermediates to a root CA in the trust store.
It must match the hostname and be within its validity dates.

sd-07-crypto-016.back:
Never commit them; load from a secret manager or environment at run time.
Scope each secret narrowly, rotate it, and revoke immediately if it leaks (git history keeps it).

sd-08-patterns-001.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-002.front: Single responsibility principle: what is the test?
sd-08-patterns-002.back:
A module should have one reason to change.
A pricer that also loads market data and writes reports changes for three reasons: split it.
sd-08-patterns-002.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-003.back: Open for extension, closed for modification: add a new product type by adding a class, not by editing every `if` chain.
sd-08-patterns-003.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-004.back:
A subtype must work anywhere its base type works, without surprising callers.
A subclass that throws on a method the base supports breaks it.
sd-08-patterns-004.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-005.back:
Core logic depends on abstractions, not on concrete IO (DB, vendor API).
Pass dependencies in (constructor or argument). Tests inject fakes; production injects real ones.
sd-08-patterns-005.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-006.back:
Inheritance couples a class to its parent's internals, and deep trees get rigid.
Composition assembles behavior from small parts that can be swapped at run time.
sd-08-patterns-006.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-007.front: Strategy pattern. Give a desk example.
sd-08-patterns-007.back:
A family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface; the caller picks one at run time.
Example: hedge-route cost models (physical, dealer swap, options) behind `cost(trade)`.
sd-08-patterns-007.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-008.back:
Create objects through a function or class that chooses the concrete type, so callers do not depend on it.
Example: build the right product object from a trade's type field.
sd-08-patterns-008.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-009.back:
Construct a complex object step by step, then build it, often validated at the end.
Useful for objects with many optional parts (e.g. a swap with optional resets, fees, DPR).
sd-08-patterns-009.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-010.back:
Wrap an incompatible interface so it matches the one your code expects.
Example: normalize two vendors' market data into one internal quote type.
sd-08-patterns-010.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-011.back:
One simple interface in front of a complex subsystem.
Example: `book_trade()` hides validation, enrichment, persistence and messaging.
sd-08-patterns-011.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-012.front: Decorator pattern, and its Python form.
sd-08-patterns-012.back:
Add behavior around an object or function without changing it.
Python decorators: `@retry`, `@cache`, `@timed` wrap a function.
sd-08-patterns-012.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-013.back:
Subscribers register for events and are notified when they occur; the publisher does not know them.
Example: pricing and risk services subscribe to market data ticks.
sd-08-patterns-013.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-014.back:
Represent a request as an object.
It can then be queued, logged, retried or undone. Examples: a write outbox; LangGraph's `Command`.
sd-08-patterns-014.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-015.front: Why model order or workflow lifecycles as explicit state machines?
sd-08-patterns-015.back:
Allowed transitions become explicit (new → partially filled → filled / cancelled), and illegal ones are rejected.
LangGraph graphs are state machines with LLM nodes.
sd-08-patterns-015.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-016.back:
Template method: a base class fixes the steps; subclasses override some (inheritance).
Strategy: the varying step is a separate object passed in (composition). Strategy is usually easier to test.
sd-08-patterns-016.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-017.front: Visitor pattern: what problem does it solve?
sd-08-patterns-017.back:
Adding operations (price, risk, report) over a fixed set of types (products) without editing each type.
Double dispatch: each product calls the visitor's method for its own type.
sd-08-patterns-017.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-018.back:
Data access behind a collection-like interface (`get`, `add`, `find`).
Domain code never sees SQL or the ORM; tests use an in-memory version.
sd-08-patterns-018.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-019.back:
Core domain logic in the center, with no IO. Ports are interfaces; adapters plug in DBs, APIs, UIs.
You can swap infrastructure without touching the core.
sd-08-patterns-019.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-020.front: Why is the singleton often an anti-pattern?
sd-08-patterns-020.back:
It is hidden global state: hard to test, hard to swap, and a source of coupling.
Prefer creating one instance at startup and injecting it.
sd-08-patterns-020.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-021.front: Value objects and immutability: why use them for trades and money?
sd-08-patterns-021.back:
Equality by value, no accidental mutation, safe to share across threads and cache.
Python: `@dataclass(frozen=True)`.
sd-08-patterns-021.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-022.front: How do you declare an interface in modern Python?
sd-08-patterns-022.back:
`typing.Protocol` (structural: any class with the right methods fits) or `abc.ABC` (nominal: must inherit).
Protocols keep adapters decoupled from your base classes.
sd-08-patterns-022.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

sd-08-patterns-023.front: DRY vs YAGNI vs KISS: how do they trade off?
sd-08-patterns-023.back:
DRY: one source of truth for each piece of knowledge.
YAGNI: do not build for imagined needs.
KISS: prefer the simple design.
Premature abstraction to stay DRY often breaks YAGNI and KISS: duplicate twice, abstract on the third.
sd-08-patterns-023.source: Gamma et al., Design Patterns (1994); Martin, SOLID; standard practice

llm-05-inference-001.front: Why can the model cache K and V of past tokens at all?
llm-05-inference-001.back:
With the causal mask, a token's K and V depend only on itself and earlier tokens.
New tokens never change them, so compute them once and store them.
llm-05-inference-001.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-002.front: What does the KV cache save, and what does it cost?
llm-05-inference-002.back:
Saves recomputing K and V for the whole prefix at every step: each new token does work for one token, not for all.
Costs GPU memory that grows linearly with context length and with the number of concurrent sequences.
llm-05-inference-002.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-003.front: Memory for model weights: rule of thumb.
llm-05-inference-003.back:
Parameters × bytes per parameter.
bf16/fp16: 2 bytes; int8/fp8: 1; int4: 0.5.
70B in bf16 = 140 GB; in int4 ≈ 35 GB (plus some overhead).
llm-05-inference-003.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-004.front: KV cache bytes per token: formula.
llm-05-inference-004.back:
$2 \times L \times h_{kv} \times d_{head} \times b$.
2 for K and V; $L$ layers; $h_{kv}$ KV heads; $d_{head}$ head dim; $b$ bytes per value.
Total = per-token × context length × concurrent sequences.
llm-05-inference-004.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-005.front: KV cache for a Llama-3-70B-style model (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, bf16). Per token? 8k context? 32 users at 8k?
llm-05-inference-005.back:
Per token: $2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 \approx 320$ KiB.
8k tokens: ≈ 2.5 GiB per sequence.
32 sequences: ≈ 80 GiB, as much as one H100 holds.
llm-05-inference-005.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-006.front: Size GPUs for serving a 70B model in bf16 to 32 users at 8k context.
llm-05-inference-006.back:
Weights 140 GB + KV ≈ 86 GB + ~10–20% overhead ≈ 250 GB.
H100 has 80 GB → at least 4 GPUs (320 GB) with tensor parallelism.
Levers: quantize weights or KV, fewer concurrent users, shorter context.
llm-05-inference-006.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-007.front: Why is single-sequence decode speed limited by memory bandwidth?
llm-05-inference-007.back:
Each new token reads all weights from GPU memory once.
Upper bound: tokens/s ≈ bandwidth / weight bytes. H100 (~3.35 TB/s), 70B bf16 (140 GB): ≈ 24 tokens/s per sequence.
llm-05-inference-007.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-008.front: Why does batching raise throughput, and what caps it?
llm-05-inference-008.back:
One weight read serves every sequence in the batch, so cost per token falls.
The cap: KV cache memory (each sequence needs its own cache), then compute.
So KV size sets how many users one GPU can serve.
llm-05-inference-008.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-009.front: Why does quantizing weights make inference faster, not only smaller?
llm-05-inference-009.back:
Decode is bandwidth-bound: fewer bytes per weight means fewer bytes read per token.
int4 reads a quarter of bf16's bytes, and frees memory for a bigger KV cache.
llm-05-inference-009.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-010.front: Which levers shrink the KV cache?
llm-05-inference-010.back:
1. GQA/MQA (fewer KV heads; built into the model).
2. KV quantization (e.g. fp8: half of bf16).
3. Shorter context or sliding-window attention.
4. Paged allocation to cut waste.
llm-05-inference-010.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-011.back:
It stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like OS memory pages, instead of one contiguous slab per sequence.
Less fragmentation and wasted reserve; shared prefixes can share blocks.
llm-05-inference-011.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-012.back:
Tensor: splits each layer's matrices across GPUs; needs fast links (NVLink); lowers latency.
Pipeline: puts different layers on different GPUs; fewer communications, but stages wait on each other.
llm-05-inference-012.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-013.front: MoE model: total vs active parameters. Which sets memory, which sets compute?
llm-05-inference-013.back:
Memory: total parameters (all experts must be loaded).
Compute per token: active parameters (only the chosen experts run).
llm-05-inference-013.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-014.front: GPU memory needed to train with Adam in mixed precision: rule of thumb.
llm-05-inference-014.back:
About 16 bytes per parameter: bf16 weights (2) + gradients (2) + fp32 master weights (4) + Adam moments (8).
70B → ≈ 1.1 TB before activations. Hence sharding (ZeRO/FSDP) across many GPUs.
llm-05-inference-014.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-015.front: How does prompt caching relate to the KV cache?
llm-05-inference-015.back:
It keeps the KV cache of a repeated prompt prefix, so the next request skips its prefill.
Cheaper and faster time to first token, if the prefix is byte-identical.
llm-05-inference-015.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

llm-05-inference-016.front: Common GPU memory sizes to remember.
llm-05-inference-016.source: Standard practice; public model configs (Llama 3); NVIDIA spec sheets; Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM)

d1-05-products-017.front: TRS at inception, one curve for discounting and projection, no dividends, zero spread. What is it worth, and why?
d1-05-products-017.back:
About 0. Under the risk-neutral measure the stock's expected total return equals the risk-free rate.
So the equity leg and the floating leg have the same value; the spread is pure margin.

d1-05-products-018.front: 10m notional, 1y, quarterly, flat 4.3% curve, spread 50 bp. Value to the client receiving equity?
d1-05-products-018.back:
About −49.4k USD (FinancePy). That is ≈ spread × notional × year fraction × discount factor.
The desk's day-one PV is the PV of the spread.

d1-05-products-019.front: Why does FinancePy's `EquitySwap.value` take three curves?
d1-05-products-019.back:
Discount curve: PV of cash flows (the collateral rate).
Index curve: projects the floating rate.
Dividend curve: expected dividends, which drive the equity forward.

d1-05-products-020.front: Which rate should drive the equity forward when a desk prices a TRS: OIS or the stock's repo/funding rate? Why?
d1-05-products-020.back:
The repo/funding rate: it is what holding the hedge actually costs.
OIS-only pricing assumes the hedge funds at OIS, which hides the funding and borrow spread from S1. The gap is why the client pays a spread.

llm-01-transformers-025.back:
It rotates queries and keys by angles that depend on position.
Then $q \cdot k$ depends on the **relative** offset between two tokens, not on their absolute positions.

llm-01-transformers-026.front: Pre-norm block: where does the normalization sit, and why?
llm-01-transformers-026.back:
Inside the branch: $x \leftarrow x + f(\text{norm}(x))$.
The residual path stays a clean identity from input to output, which keeps deep stacks trainable. (The 2017 paper normalized after the sum.)
llm-01-transformers-026.source: Vaswani et al. 2017; pre-norm as in GPT-2

llm-01-transformers-027.front: Transformer MLP: shape, and its share of a block's parameters.
llm-01-transformers-027.back:
$d \to 4d \to d$ with a nonlinearity in the middle.
About $8d^2$ parameters, against $4d^2$ for attention: roughly **2/3** of the block.

llm-01-transformers-028.front: What is perplexity? Give it for a model that puts $p = 0{.}25$ on each correct token.
llm-01-transformers-028.back:
Perplexity $= e^{L}$: the effective number of equally likely choices per token.
$L = -\ln 0{.}25 = 1{.}39$, so perplexity $= 4$.

llm-01-transformers-029.front: Embedding table: its shape, and what a sentence of $n$ tokens becomes.
llm-01-transformers-029.back:
$E$: $(\text{vocab}, d)$. Token id $i$ picks row $i$.
The sentence becomes $X$: $(n, d)$, one row per token.

llm-01-transformers-030.front: For $n$ tokens: shape of $QK^\top$ and of the attention output.
llm-01-transformers-030.back:
$QK^\top$: $(n, n)$ per head. Row = the token that asks; column = the token that is read.
Output: $(n, d_v)$, one row per token.

llm-01-transformers-031.front: Attention softmax: over which axis, and what sums to 1?
llm-01-transformers-031.back:
Over each **row** of the score matrix.
For each token that asks, its weights over the tokens it reads sum to 1.

llm-01-transformers-032.front: With a causal mask, what is the attention output of the first token?
llm-01-transformers-032.back:
Its own value, $v_1$.
It sees only itself, and the softmax of a single score gives weight 1.

llm-01-transformers-033.front: In training, how many next-token predictions does one sequence of $n$ tokens give, and why?
llm-01-transformers-033.back:
$n$: one per position, in a single forward pass.
The causal mask stops each position from seeing its own answer, so all positions train at once.

llm-03-agents-025.front: What does a reranker do in RAG, and what does it cost?
llm-03-agents-025.back:
A cross-encoder reads the query and each candidate chunk **together** and rescores the top results.
Higher precision than embedding similarity, but one model call per candidate: use it only on the top few dozen.

llm-03-agents-026.front: After a tool runs, how does its result reach the model?
llm-03-agents-026.back:
The app appends it to the conversation as a tool-result message, linked to the call by an id.
The model then sees the whole history again and decides the next step.

llm-03-agents-027.front: Per-step success 99%, 10 dependent steps: chance the run succeeds? And at 95% with 20 steps?
llm-03-agents-027.back:
$0.99^{10} \approx 90\%$.
$0.95^{20} \approx 36\%$.
Both the per-step rate and the chain length matter.

llm-04-langgraph-018.front: Two nodes run in one super-step; one fails. What happens on resume?
llm-04-langgraph-018.back:
The successful node's writes were saved as **pending writes**.
On resume only the failed node runs again; the successful one is not recomputed.

llm-04-langgraph-019.front: LangGraph durability modes: name the three and the trade-off.
llm-04-langgraph-019.back:
`"exit"`: persist only when the run exits. Fastest; no recovery mid-run.
`"async"`: persist while the next step runs. Small risk of losing a checkpoint on a crash.
`"sync"`: persist before the next step starts. Safest, slowest.

llm-04-langgraph-020.back:
Like an update from a node: values go through the key's reducer.
So a key with `operator.add` **appends**; it does not overwrite. It creates a new checkpoint (a fork); the old one stays.

llm-04-langgraph-021.front: State `{"items": ["a"], "n": 1}`; `items` uses `operator.add`, `n` has no reducer. A node returns `{"items": ["b"], "n": 5}`. New state?
llm-04-langgraph-021.back:
`{"items": ["a", "b"], "n": 5}`.
`items` is appended by its reducer; `n` is overwritten (the default).
